#4805. Braiins warns of Bitcoin mining attacks affecting over 1,000 sites

Bitcoin mining pool operator Braiins warned that attackers are exploiting unsecured connections to hijack miners’ computing power and potentially steal rewards.

Bitcoin mining pool operator Braiins has warned of a growing security threat to the Bitcoin mining industry after a series of attacks affected more than 1,000 mining sites.

In a report shared on Wednesday, Braiins said an attacker redirected internet traffic between Bitcoin miners and their mining pools, allowing the attacker to claim credit for work done by someone else’s machines.

The company identified 24 incidents between Nov. 7 and 20, with the amount of computing power affected in a single attack increasing nearly elevenfold over two weeks. “The episodes so far were short, but they grew from under 175 PH/s to 1.9 EH/s in two weeks,” Braiins said.

Bitcoin’s total computing power, known as hashrate, stood at an estimated 1,016 exahashes per second (EH/s) on Nov. 20, according to MineOrNot data. For context, the computing power affected in the largest attack was equivalent to about 0.19% of that total.

Braiins’ report underscores how the widespread use of unsecured connections could leave more Bitcoin miners vulnerable to similar attacks in the future.

Related: Luxor CEO warns of AI ‘dark forest’ following Bitcoin miner hijack

The attacks exploited a weakness in Stratum V1, a widely used mining protocol introduced in 2012 that allows mining machines to communicate with mining pools.

However, the unsecured version does not let miners check whether they are connected to the right pool. This allows attackers to basically impersonate mining pools and collect Bitcoin (BTC) rewards at miners’ expense.

The earlier incidents mainly affected mining sites in Brazil and Argentina. But four larger attacks on Nov. 20 each affected between 1,050 and 1,600 mining sites, mostly in Europe.

While Braiins did not specify whether the attacks affected large commercial mining farms or smaller independent miners, it said the vast majority of Bitcoin’s computing power still uses unsecured Stratum V1 connections.

The attacks come as Bitcoin miners are already facing pressure from lower Bitcoin prices and high operating costs, with several major mining companies pivoting to artificial intelligence (AI) and data center services for new avenues of revenue.

Miners may not immediately notice the attacks because their machines continue to run, the report said. This means they could continue paying for electricity while simultaneously losing mining earnings.

Braiins said neither its mining pool nor the affected machines were hacked directly. The company also did not disclose how much money miners may have lost.

On Nov. 23, Braiins reviewed the largest Bitcoin mining pools and found that most still only offered unsecured Stratum V1 connections.

The company urged miners to switch to Stratum V2, a newer version that protects communications and allows miners to check that they are connected to the right pool.

Meanwhile, miners who cannot upgrade can still use Stratum V1 if their pool offers an encrypted connection and their mining software can verify the pool’s identity.

The warning comes after Bitcoin mining services provider Luxor Technology suffered a separate attack earlier this month.

As Cointelegraph reported on Nov. 16, attackers exploited a weakness in Luxor’s mining management software, Commander, to redirect customers’ computing power to the OCEAN mining pool. The attack affected a little over a dozen customer accounts.

Luxor said it fixed the issue within two hours of detecting the unauthorized changes and also promised to fully compensate affected customers.

#4804. Elon Musk’s SpaceX Gets FCC Approval to Launch AI Data Centers in Space

Elon Musk’s SpaceX Gets FCC Approval to Launch AI Data Centers in Space

The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) on Wednesday authorized SpaceX to deploy up to one million satellites designed to operate as data centers in space, giving Elon Musk the regulatory green light to pursue one of his most ambitious artificial intelligence projects yet.

The constellation, called Starmind, will consist of solar-powered computing modules designed to process large amounts of data in orbit for use back on Earth. It marks the first time the U.S. regulator has authorized a satellite constellation specifically designed for this purpose.

The FCC even brought a bit of science fiction into its announcement, suggesting the project could bring humanity closer to becoming a Kardashev Type II civilization—a hypothetical society capable of harnessing the entire energy output of its star.

SpaceX originally submitted its proposal in January, with the FCC opening a review in February, shortly after Musk folded his AI startup xAI, the developer of Grok, into SpaceX.

Unlike Starlink satellites, which primarily provide internet connectivity, Starmind satellites would perform computations themselves, exchanging information through laser communications. The authorization also allows SpaceX to use radio frequencies as a backup for communications and emergency satellite controls.

Electricity has become one of the biggest bottlenecks in the AI industry. Companies can spend billions of dollars building data centers and buying chips, only to find that local power grids cannot supply enough electricity to run them.

Satellites operating in certain orbits can receive sunlight almost continuously, making solar panels up to eight times more productive than their counterparts on Earth, according to Google research.

Google is pursuing a similar initiative called Project Suncatcher. The company launched its first prototype in October and selected Blue Origin, Jeff Bezos’ space company, for another mission scheduled for 2029.

Keeping computers cool in space, despite its reputation for being extremely cold, is surprisingly difficult. The vacuum prevents heat from dissipating through air, meaning satellites need radiators to expel the heat generated by AI chips, which must also withstand exposure to cosmic radiation.

There are environmental concerns, too. The Center for Space Environmentalism warned in September that manufacturing, deploying and eventually deorbiting a constellation of this size could contribute significantly to atmospheric pollution. The FCC said Starmind complies with its orbital debris regulations.

Getting permission to launch a million satellites and actually putting them in orbit are two very different things. During an investment conference earlier this month, Musk estimated that the first Starmind computers could launch in the third quarter of 2027.

SpaceX’s securities disclosures have previously warned investors that its orbital computing business has yet to demonstrate commercial viability and could ultimately prove unsuccessful.

In a letter sent to SEC Chair Atkins, Sens. Warren and Van Hollen said the agency's "Regulation Crypto Assets" would allow crypto firms to circumvent securities laws.

Top Democrats Sen. Elizabeth Warren and Chris Van Hollen are demanding that Securities and Exchange Commission Chair Paul Atkins take down its crypto rulemaking governing how crypto projects can raise capital and how tokenized securities can be traded.

In two separate letters sent to Atkins on Tuesday, Sens. Warren, Van Hollen and Tina Smith and other Senate Banking Committee members said the agency's "Regulation Crypto Assets" would allow crypto firms to circumvent securities laws, weaken state jurisdiction and could harm investors.

"The proposal would create a new 'tailored securities offering regime' for certain investment contracts involving crypto assets," the senators wrote. "However, the proposal only serves to help crypto assets escape from the SEC's regulatory regime and gives them special treatment—with less oversight—compared to other traditional securities."

In August, the SEC proposed crypto offering rules to offer startup and fundraising exemptions for digital asset offerings. It allows for a "startup exemption" that would exempt offerings of up to $5 million from registration rules under the Securities Act of 1933 for four years — a federal law focused on anti-fraud and requiring certain disclosures. The proposal also includes a "fundraising exemption" for offerings up to $75 million for a year.

Warren is poised to take on a more prominent role following Democrats’ victories in November's midterm elections, which handed the party control of both chambers of Congress. Warren has been critical of crypto in the past and has particularly brought up concerns around illicit finance and money laundering. Meanwhile, Van Hollen could be the next Senate Majority Leader. He has since challenged current Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer for that role.

Sens. Jack Reed and Tina Smith join the two in the second letter asking the SEC to withdraw its innovation exemption — a measure released in September to bring capital markets onchain through the trading of tokenized stocks. It is a five-year exemption that would exempt certain trading venues, called tokenized securities venues, from being defined as an exchange and also exempts specific liquidity providers from being defined as a dealer under securities law when they trade stocks or provide liquidity through automated market makers.

The senators said it would allow platforms to operate outside of certain safeguards, including involving fair pricing and market transparency.

"The order would allow TSV platforms to operate a shadow stock market outside longstanding regulatory protections designed to ensure fair and transparent markets, impose new burdens on publicly traded companies seeking to protect their shareholders, and create unnecessary risks of illicit financial activity," the senators wrote.

The three senators also said the innovation exemption could cause capital markets to splinter.

"As concerned stakeholders have pointed out, fragmenting our securities markets by creating a lightly regulated alternative marketplace for tokenized securities unnecessarily risks dividing liquidity into isolated pools and expanding opportunities for corrosive regulatory arbitrage," they said.

A separate group of Senate Democrats have also brought up concerns about the innovation exemption. Last week, Sens. Angela Alsobrooks, Ruben Gallego, Mark Warner and Catherine Cortez Masto said it could open the door for illicit finance actors and also had concerns about protections for retail investors around pricing.

#4801. Voyager 1 is officially one light-day away from Earth

🛍️ 200+ Black Friday deals actually worth buying 🛍️

Updated Nov 19, 2026 9:53 AM EST

After traveling through space for almost 50 years, NASA’s Voyager 1 spacecraft should be one light-day away from Earth. The probe reached this record-breaking milestone at approximately 5:16:07 a.m. EST on Wednesday, November 18. Since takes about 24 hours to receive any signal from Voyager 1, NASA officially confirmed that it reached the distance on Thursday, November 19.

William Kurth, a research scientist at the University of Iowa who has worked on the Voyager mission since 1974 tells Popular Science that this mission is about more than just science.

“The Voyager missions represent humanity’s curiosity and hunger to understand our species’ place in the universe,” he says. “They show that we are explorers and can work together to do wonderful things.”

Astronomers often describe vast cosmic distances in light-years. It’s arguably the most famous unit of measurement when talking about the universe, in part because of its sheer incomprehensibility. A single particle of light travels at a speed of about 186,282 miles per second. Hypothetically speaking, if you fired a beam of light into the night sky at the outset of reading this story, it would travel around 44.7 million miles into space by the time you finished.

But even a unit like a light-minute isn’t particularly useful to astronomers. For them, cosmic measurements only start making sense on a scale of light-years. Voyager 1 is nowhere close to a light-year away from Earth, but a light-day (approximately 16,094,799,105 miles) is still basically impossible to envision as a distance. And since radio communications travel at nearly the speed of light, any messages to and from the spacecraft will require about 24 (Earth) hours to receive.

“Voyager 1 crossing the light-day threshold is yet another historic feat on an extraordinary voyage of discovery,” Dave Gallagher, the director of NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory, said in an emailed statement confirming the milestone. “Above all, this milestone stands as a testament to the exceptional teams who built, programmed, and fly these spacecraft today, and who have overcome countless challenges to keep them connected to Earth across the vastness of space. As NASA pushes toward new frontiers in human and robotic exploration, Voyager and the people behind its success continue to inspire us to reach farther and dream bigger.”

Even at one light-day from Earth, Voyager 1 isn’t done just yet. While several of its instruments are no longer functioning, it still routinely sends back invaluable information from its vantage point beyond the solar system.

“Voyager 1 is telling us about our sun’s interaction with its galactic neighborhood. It has told us about the amount of galactic cosmic rays, unfiltered by the sun’s magnetic field,” says Kurth. “We are learning about the variation of plasma density in the interstellar medium just outside the heliosphere (sun’s extended atmosphere). We’re anxious to see where the direction of the magnetic field rotates from one similar to the heliospheric direction to that of the pristine interstellar medium.”

“Though it might be a long shot, I hope to see Voyager 1 crossing into the predicted hot hydrogen wall,” Adam Szabo, a Project Investigator on Voyager’s Magnetometer Experiment, tells Popular Science. “The wall is composed of neutral hydrogen atoms, so it will not register easily, but it must have some magnetic and plasma wave signature.”

Voyager 1 launched on September 5, 1977, heading for Jupiter and Saturn. Voyager 1 has 10 scientific instruments onboard, including two Golden Records engraved with sights, sounds, and depictions of life on Earth onboard—should the probe encounter any extraterrestrial life.

In March 1979, the Voyager 1 discovered a thin ring around Jupiter and two new Jovian moons: Thebe and Metis. When it reached Saturn in 1980, the spacecraft spotted five new moons and a new ring called the G-ring.

As part of a concept that NASA called the Grand Tour, the Voyager mission as a whole took advantage of a once-every-175-year alignment of the outer planets for a grand tour of the solar system. Its twin spacecraft Voyager 2 later explored Neptune and Uranus.

On February 17, 1998, Voyager 1 became the furthest human-made object in space, after overtaking NASA’s Pioneer 10 probe. It crossed into interstellar space in August 2012, and became the first spacecraft to cross the heliosphere. This boundary is where the influences from outside of our solar system are stronger than those from our sun.

All good things must come to an end, of course. Voyager 1 is powered by three radioisotope thermoelectric generators (RTGs) fueled by decaying plutonium-23. The isotope possesses a 87.74-year half-life, so the batteries are currently operating at around two-thirds their original strength. NASA has slowly shut down onboard equipment in recent years to conserve energy, but there will come a time when there simply isn’t enough left in the RTGs for anything to operate. Barring any technical issues, mission engineers expect to bid Voyager 1 a final farewell sometime during the 2030s.

The spacecraft may cease its work as a cosmic laboratory, but its very existence ensures it will remain a monument to humanity’s potential as it barrels forward for eons.

“Voyager 1 and its companion Voyager 2 have taught us time and again that nature is not as simple and predictable as we thought,” Kurth explains. “Voyager has always provided surprising differences from our best guesses as to what it will see in any new region.”

Additionally, Szabo adds that it has an important lesson for anyone on Earth who has ever had a dream.

“Do not be afraid to dream big. In 1977, even the Grand Tour seemed like a long shot,” he says. “We did not even conceive of making it into interstellar space. Dream big.”

UPDATE November 19 10:00 a.m. EST: An earlier version of this story said light moves at 186,282 feet per second. It is 186,282 miles per second. We have updated unit of measurement and apologize for the error.

#4799. Switzerland clears 57 jurisdictions for crypto tax data sharing

The move paves the way for Switzerland to exchange crypto tax data with foreign authorities starting in 2028 as part of a global effort to combat tax evasion.

Switzerland’s Federal Council has approved 57 potential partner jurisdictions for the automatic exchange of information on crypto assets starting in 2028, a move that would expand tax authorities’ access to information on taxpayers’ crypto activity across borders.

According to a Wednesday announcement, the approved jurisdictions include all European Union member states, the United Kingdom and several G20 countries. Switzerland will only share information with jurisdictions that express interest and meet international standards for confidentiality and data security.

Switzerland had initially planned to introduce crypto tax reporting requirements in 2026 but delayed implementation by at least a year as lawmakers had yet to determine which jurisdictions the country would exchange information with. Under the revised timeline, crypto service providers could begin collecting data as early as Jan. 1, 2027, with the first exchanges between tax authorities taking place in 2028.

The reporting requirements fall under the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development’s (OECD) Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework (CARF), which aims to combat tax evasion by requiring crypto exchanges and other covered service providers to report customer identities, tax residency and transaction data to tax authorities.

The crypto reporting framework is designed to supplement Switzerland’s existing system for exchanging financial account information and close gaps in tax transparency, according to the State Secretariat for International Finance. Switzerland introduced the legal framework for that system in 2017 and exchanged financial account data with 113 jurisdictions in 2026.

The European Union introduced crypto reporting requirements under the OECD framework in January, with the first international exchanges of information scheduled for 2027. As of March, 76 jurisdictions worldwide had committed to exchanging information under CARF, according to the European Commission.

#4798. House Committee advances Strategic Bitcoin Reserve bill with narrow path to passage

Looking for institutional-grade crypto trading? Discover LMAX Digital, the regulated exchange from LMAX Group

The current 119th Congress is expected to adjourn in the coming weeks, leaving little time for a House floor vote, Senate consideration, and final passage before the session ends.

The House Financial Services Committee has advanced H.R. 8957, the American Reserve Modernization Act of 2026, which would codify a Strategic Bitcoin Reserve and impose a minimum 20-year lock on federally held bitcoin Bitcoin (BTC).

The legislation, introduced on May 21 by Rep. Nick Begich, would allow the Treasury secretary to establish a Strategic Bitcoin Reserve and a separate Digital Asset Stockpile for other cryptocurrencies 180 days after enactment.

Once deposited in the reserve, bitcoin cannot be "sold, swapped, auctioned, encumbered, or otherwise disposed of for any purpose" for at least 20 years. The bill also includes transparency requirements such as proof-of-reserve reporting and directs federal agencies to report existing holdings.

On Sept. 16, the House Financial Services Committee approved it on a party-line vote of 28-21, with support from every Republican representative and opposition from every Democrat. On Nov. 24, the committee officially sent the revised bill to the full House, where it is now eligible for a floor vote.

The bill builds on U.S. President Donald Trump's executive order issued in March 2025 that directed the creation of a bitcoin reserve funded mainly through bitcoin already owned by the government from criminal or civil forfeitures, and a separate digital asset stockpile. The order sparked concern from some lawmakers on bitcoin's riskiness and volatility.

While the bill is now on the Union Calendar as Calendar No. 789, its chances of passing are low. The current 119th Congress is expected to adjourn in the coming weeks, leaving little time for a House floor vote, Senate consideration, and final passage before the session ends.

Polymarket odds show a 4% chance of the U.S. establishing a national bitcoin reserve by the end of this year, down from 60% around a year ago and 34% in May this year.

If the bill fails to pass within this Congress, it would have to be reintroduced in the 120th Congress. The Strategic Bitcoin Reserve created by the March 2025 executive order would remain in place, but a future president could alter or reverse it without congressional approval. Reintroducing and advancing the initiative may face steeper challenges as Democrats are set to control both chambers starting in January.

#4797. Tesla needs wireless charging fast, or its $30,000 Cybercab can’t charge at home

Tesla is now taking orders for the $29,990 Cybercab, with the first deliveries expected in Austin next month. But there’s a problem buyers should know about: they won’t be able to charge it at home.

The Cybercab has no onboard charger, so it only takes DC fast charging. And the wireless home charging pad Tesla has been teasing since 2023 still isn’t something you can buy.

When Tesla unveiled the Cybercab in 2024, Elon Musk said it wouldn’t even have a plug. “It just goes over the inductive charger and charges,” he said on stage.

That plan didn’t survive production, or at least the current version in production. Cybercabs have a NACS charge port behind a panel in the rear bumper, and Tesla has been plugging Cybercabs into regular Superchargers in Austin since they joined the fleet.

The bigger issue is what sits behind that port. Tesla confirmed to attendees at Tesla’s Austin launch event in September that Cybercab has no onboard charger, the box that turns the AC power coming out of your wall into DC power the battery can store.

No onboard charger means no Wall Connector. No Mobile Connector on a 120V outlet, and no Level 2 station at the mall either. If it isn’t a DC fast charger, the Cybercab can’t use it.

For a robotaxi, deleting the onboard charger makes sense. It’s one less part to buy, cool, and carry around, and a fleet car spends its downtime at a depot, not in someone’s garage. Those little things help make the car more economical and efficient.

But Tesla is now selling the Cybercab to individuals.

As we reported last week, Tesla’s Cybercab autonomy agreement requires a $299 monthly subscription for the car to move at all. The same document puts charging squarely on the buyer: “You are responsible for registration, insurance, parking, charging, general cleaning and all other costs.”

It also tells owners to “keep the vehicle charged and connected so over-the-air updates can install.” Connected to what, it doesn’t say.

The Cybercab Order Agreement limits the car to NACS DC fast charging, Superchargers included. It also says only the registered owner can use the Cybercab, and only while physically present in it for the entire trip.

The subscription agreement carves out one exception: when service is due, the Cybercab “will travel autonomously, unoccupied to a Tesla service center.” Nothing similar exists for charging.

So you can’t send your Cybercab to a Supercharger at 2 a.m. while you sleep, which is the one thing a self-driving car should be great at. You’d have to ride along, sit in a two-seater at a Supercharger while it charges, and ride back home.

The obvious answer is the wireless home charger Tesla keeps promising.

Tesla first showed what looked like a wireless home charging station during its Investor Day in March 2023. Later that year, chief designer Franz von Holzhausen confirmed the project on Jay Leno’s Garage, saying owners would “just drive over the pad in your garage” to start charging.

Tesla then filed patents for the charging pad and, after the Cybercab unveiling, released a video of it charging the robotaxi at 25 kW, claiming efficiency “well above 90%.” In February, the FCC granted Tesla a waiver to use ultra-wideband radios to guide the Cybercab onto the pad.

And that’s where it stops. Tesla has never sold the pad, never priced it, and never given it a launch date. It even gave up on wireless charging for the Cybertruck last year, even though the truck shipped with the connectors for it.

With deliveries estimated for December, Tesla has about six weeks to launch a home pad if it wants the first owners to charge in their own garage.

Tesla’s own plans for Cybercab charging revolve around fleet depots. In Austin, it filed plans for a hub on St. Elmo Road with 48 V4 Supercharger stalls in a first phase and cabinets to support 80 wireless chargers in a second.

Tesla could, in theory, let private owners use it. But with the owner-presence rule, that means riding to a depot across town and waiting there. That’s a Supercharger visit with extra steps.

The other route is a home DC charger, and those exist. We covered Sigenergy’s 25 kW bidirectional DC charging module last year, which bypasses a car’s onboard charger the same way a Supercharger does. Lunar Energy also announced a 25 kW home DC charger this year, but it’s not expected until mid-2027.

Neither is a plug-and-play answer. Sigenergy’s module is built to sit inside its SigenStor home battery system, which isn’t cheap, and Tesla would have to support third-party DC charging on a car it controls this tightly. Tesla could also build its own small DC wall unit. It hasn’t announced one, but CEO Elon Musk talked about integrating one into the Powerwall for years.

This is what happens when you take a vehicle designed for a fleet and sell it to consumers to hit a deadline. And let’s be honest, charging is probably not even in the top 5 of problems with selling the Cybercab to personal owners in its current state.

Musk promised a Cybercab would be sold to a customer for under $30,000 before 2027. Technically, he’s going to make it. But on the Q3 earnings call, he also said “the vast majority” of Cybercabs will stay Tesla-owned and run as transport-as-a-service. The car was clearly engineered around that, and deleting the onboard charger is the best example.

That saved Tesla money on every unit. The cost now lands on the few people buying one.

I don't see any evidence that the production Cybercab has the onboard hardware to use such a pad. Besides the wireless receiver coil it would need some kind of charging hardware to convert the pulsed wireless charging into DC to charge the battery.

If you live in Austin next to a Supercharger, you’ll manage. But think about what Tesla is actually selling here: a self-driving car that can’t drive itself to charge, can’t charge in your garage, and needs you sitting in it at a Supercharger. That’s worse than owning a Model 3 with a Wall Connector, and it costs $299 a month on top.

#4796. Nvidia to Pay $290 Million to Settle Long-Running Crypto Mining Revenue Lawsuit

Nvidia to Pay $290 Million to Settle Long-Running Crypto Mining Revenue Lawsuit

Nvidia has agreed to pay $290 million to settle a shareholder lawsuit dating back to 2018, resolving long-running claims that the chipmaker misled investors about how much of its soaring gaming revenue was actually driven by cryptocurrency miners.

According to a court filing Tuesday, the proposed cash settlement would close a case rooted in the 2017-2018 crypto boom, when miners snapped up Nvidia’s GeForce GPUs to mint coins, with the sales booked as gaming revenue.

As Decrypt reported, shareholders alleged Nvidia downplayed its dependence on that volatile mining demand, leaving investors blindsided when the boom collapsed.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short Nvidia with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

In November 2018, the company cut its quarterly revenue forecast as mining demand evaporated, and its stock tumbled roughly 28% over the following two trading sessions.

The settlement covers investors who bought Nvidia stock between Aug. 10, 2017, and Nov. 15, 2018. An analysis commissioned by the plaintiffs estimated Nvidia had understated its crypto-related GPU sales by about $1.1 billion over that stretch.

The company has consistently denied wrongdoing, arguing it could not reliably quantify how much of its gaming revenue stemmed from mining, and it is not admitting liability as part of the deal.

The case has taken a winding, years-long path through the courts. A district court dismissed the suit in March 2021 for failure to adequately allege the executives knew they were misleading investors. A federal appeals court then partly revived it in 2023, keeping the claims alive against Nvidia and CEO Jensen Huang while dismissing those against two other executives, including Colette Kress, the finance chief who briefly served as interim CEO during Huang’s recent ouster.

The dispute then reached the U.S. Supreme Court, which heard arguments before dismissing the appeal in December 2024 without ruling on the merits. The district court certified the class in March 2026, and the $290 million figure emerged from mediation led by former federal judge Layn Phillips, whose recommendation both sides accepted in September.

The sum is modest for a company whose market value has swelled into the trillions on the AI boom.

Plaintiffs’ damages expert pegged the maximum the class could have won at trial at about $2.06 billion, meaning the settlement represents roughly 14% of those potential damages, a figure the plaintiffs’ lawyers note compares favorably with typical securities-case recoveries.

Those attorneys said they plan to seek up to 21.4% of the fund, or about $62 million, in legal fees, which they stressed sits below the Ninth Circuit’s 25% benchmark.

The settlement still requires court approval. Under the plaintiffs’ proposed schedule, the court would first decide whether to grant preliminary approval and send notice to affected shareholders, with a final settlement hearing to follow about 130 days later.

Notably, the deal is unrelated to the separate, far more recent turmoil around Nvidia and CEO Jensen Huang, whose brief ouster and reinstatement this month over a spy-tinged scandal rattled markets.

For Nvidia, the agreement finally draws a line under one of the last major legal hangovers from crypto’s last great mining frenzy.

Galaxy now treats a daily close below $58,525, the June 30 closing low, as the start of a move toward a materially lower low.

Galaxy has withdrawn its October call that bitcoin's bear market ended in June, warning that the world's largest cryptocurrency could move even lower when it breaks the June level.

In a research note released Wednesday, Alex Thorn, head of firmwide research at Galaxy, wrote that the team's previous technical argument is "no longer valid" and that the team now treats a daily close below $58,525 — the June 30 closing low — as the start of a move toward a materially lower low.

Galaxy's revised outlook comes as the crypto market remained volatile. Bitcoin Bitcoin (BTC) rose 2.4% over the past 24 hours to trade at $60,677 as of 10:50 p.m. ET Wednesday, after falling to as low as around $57,300 earlier in the day, according to The Block's BTC price page. Ethereum Ethereum (ETH) climbed 2.1% to $1,695, BNB gained 3.2%, and XRP added 4.2%.

Last month, Thorn had suggested that bitcoin's bear market ended in June. He cited Galaxy's September reclaim of the 50-week moving average, a level that has historically served as a ceiling during bear markets. However, Thorn's latest note points out that after seven weekly closes above the average, bitcoin closed back below it in early November and later closed below the 200-week average.

"[Although] bitcoin has until about Dec. 8 to regain the average, we must acknowledge that the bear market is very likely not over and that the reclaim is unlikely to come in time," Thorn said in the note. "Previously, no reclaim of this kind had been followed by a new low."

Galaxy said that a daily close below $58,525 would be a "break of a standing low," adding that in all seven prior bear markets when bitcoin broke a similar standing low, the prices fell at least another 17%.

The firm also noted that the macro backdrop has deteriorated since June. On Nov. 19, the two-year Treasury yield was 0.88 percentage point above the fed funds rate — "a sign that the market is pricing a higher policy rate ahead," Thorn said. Also, the S&P 500 was 1.5% below its record at the June low and closed 11.6% below it on Nov. 20, according to the report.

U.S. spot bitcoin exchange-traded products have shed 71,339 BTC ($4.95 billion) since Oct. 4, with outflows on 22 of 35 sessions, according to Galaxy. That left holdings at an estimated 1.24 million BTC, 9.7% below the Oct. 9, 2025, peak.

"Whether Jensen Huang's return to Nvidia on Nov. 23 can be the spark that pulls bitcoin back up to levels needed to end the bear market is unknown," Thorn added.

Thorn said traders should watch whether bitcoin can hold its June lows of $58,525 on a daily close and $59,517 on a weekly closing basis. "A weekly close back above the 200-week average, then the 50-week average, would bring us back toward our October view," Thorn said.

Beyond the technical levels, the firm is also watching whether financial advisors increase their bitcoin ETP holdings and whether the two-year Treasury yield moves back toward the fed funds rate.

#4793. Prickly pears can generate solar electricity

🛍️ 200+ Black Friday deals actually worth buying 🛍️

Published Nov 19, 2026 11:00 AM EST

Most plants rely on real-time photosynthesis for food, which means they aren’t generating energy unless the sun is out. Meanwhile, cacti like the prickly pear must get creative in order to survive the harsh conditions they live in. With high temperatures and little water, these plants and similar species like aloe and pineapple evolved a specialized process called crassulacean acid metabolism (CAM). The overall principles are the same, but instead of converting carbon dioxide (CO₂) and water into sugars solely during daylight, CAM allows a prickly pear to extend its photosynthesis over a full 24 hours.

Plants generally absorb carbon dioxide through pores in their leaves, but the prickly pear can’t afford such an evolutionary luxury. The desert heat would turn those same tiny openings into water drains. With CAM, a prickly pear only absorbs carbon dioxide at night, and subsequently turns it into malic acid. Photosynthesis later breaks down the acid—but only on the side of the plant directly exposed to sunlight. The shady side retains its malic acid, creating a pH concentration gradient. Interestingly, this pH imbalance is also one of the underlying principles for generating electricity…see where this is going?

Environmental biologists certainly did. In a study published today in the journal Plants, People, Planet, a team at the University of California, Santa Cruz, (UC Santa Cruz) detailed a new, interdisciplinary system that transforms the common prickly pear into a green solar panel. Although prickly pear voltages aren’t enough to deliver a noticeable jolt, they are strong enough to power the tiny sensors often used by farmers to monitor their crops. With some additional fine-tuning, their novel methods could offer a promising, sustainable adaptation to ongoing climate concerns.

“It was just so nice to have 10 students in a room from all across campus working together on a single project. When we’re looking at climate solutions, that’s what we need,” Charlie Chesney, a UC Santa Cruz environmental scientist and study co-author, said in a statement.

Wiring a single spiky plant doesn’t do much, but linking them together adds up. As few as eight prickly pears are enough to generate 4.5 volts of electricity—nearly three times the charge of a commercial AA battery. That’s more than enough to power the common, low-energy sensors used to assess plants.

“There are many commercial applications of cacti [for] monitoring their health using a low-power system like ours, that is just operating off on the side and is self-powered,” explained UC Santa Cruz ecologist and study co-author Michael Loik.

He offered one such scenario, where wired prickly pears function as organic “sentinels” that monitor field conditions and relay the information back to a farmer’s office.

“This could be a really interesting avenue to pursue,” he added.

The idea isn’t limited to the prickly pear, either. Any plant that uses CAM—aloe, pineapple, agave—could benefit from a similar battery upgrade. The team even assessed how the cacti performed under a standard desert challenge like drought. Even after 15 months without water, sample prickly pears weren’t simply surviving—they were still photosynthesizing. In some cases, the resultant voltages were higher than watered control plants.

“This was a really surprising result, but also showed how resilient a cactus is—it could still produce electricity even when it seems, to us, like it’s near death,” added Chesney.

#4791. AI labs likely sitting on cryptography ‘bombshells,’ computer scientist says

AI is driving a massive wave of mathematical breakthroughs which could have implications for cryptography.

Theoretical computer scientist Scott Aaronson says leading AI laboratories are likely sitting on undisclosed breakthroughs in cryptography.

In a blog post on Wednesday, Aaronson, a former OpenAI researcher and professor at The University of Texas at Austin, warned that algorithms emerging from AI-driven mathematical advances will eventually break currently deployed cryptosystems.

“I’m virtually certain, from multiple reliable sources, that the AI labs are now sitting on one or more bombshells in that area,” Aaronson said. “However, until I either see details or hear directly from someone at a lab, I feel much, much less confident about the specific nature of those bombshells.”

The remarks add to concerns that AI’s accelerating mathematical capabilities could eventually undermine the cryptography used to secure crypto wallets and blockchain transactions. Ethereum co-founder Vitalik Buterin and researcher Justin Drake raised those concerns in October.

Recent weeks have illustrated the pace at which AI has been able to overcome previously unsolvable math problems.

On Friday, Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge released an AI-assisted proof of the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, one of the most famous unsolved problems in mathematics.

Alpöge developed it with an unreleased version of Claude over roughly six weeks, spanning 17 million lines of Lean code. The proof was later verified as correct by Lean FRO and the Mathlib Initiative.

Days later, both Anthropic and OpenAI released proofs of the VP versus VNP conjecture, described as an algebraic cousin of P versus NP, another major unsolved problem in theoretical computer science.

In October, OpenAI released 722 AI-generated math manuscripts covering 372 problem areas on GitHub, which has since been nicknamed the “mathocalypse.”

“This past week — is very much like I would’ve always imagined the beginning of an AI singularity to look and feel like,” said Aaronson.

Related: AI poses greater threat to Bitcoin than quantum computing, Swan founder says

One of the rumors, according to Aaronson, is that one or both of the AI labs have solved “Factoring in P,” referring to a polynomial-time factoring algorithm — a breakthrough that could threaten RSA cryptography.

AI commentator Andrew Curran and Carnegie Mellon University machine learning researcher Aran Nayebi also said they had heard similar rumors.

Aaronson, however, declined to offer any insight on the idea that ECDSA, a digital signature scheme used by Bitcoin, had been broken.

“Crucially, don’t want the cryptography part of the story to overshadow the intellectual enormity of what’s happening,” said Aaronson.

“If, in these days of long-prophesied revelation and wonders and terrors, your main worry is your Bitcoin wallet, then go somewhere else for rumors about whether or not ECDSA is broken or whatever. I don’t have what you’re looking for here.”

Looking for institutional-grade crypto trading? Discover LMAX Digital, the regulated exchange from LMAX Group

BIT Asset Management's BBIT fund debuted on SIX Swiss Exchange with 350 BTC in assets and a 0.19% annual expense ratio.

BIT Asset Management's spot bitcoin ETF has begun trading on the SIX Swiss Exchange, with the company saying it is the first ETF in Switzerland to hold bitcoin directly.

The fund trades under the ticker BBIT in U.S. dollars and Swiss francs. It debuted with 350 BTC (currently worth over $20 million) in assets and has a total expense ratio of 0.19% a year. BIT said BBIT is currently Europe's only spot bitcoin ETF.

The Jacobi FT Wilshire Bitcoin ETF was Europe's first spot bitcoin ETF when it debuted on Euronext Amsterdam in August 2023. Euronext has listed the fund as inactive since Feb. 2, 2026. Jacobi Asset Management (Holdings) Ltd appointed a liquidator on Feb. 26, 2026, as part of a creditors' voluntary liquidation, according to a notice in The Gazette.

BBIT is publicly offered only in Switzerland. BIT pointed to investors outside the U.S., including Asian investors who hold assets with Swiss private banks, as a potential audience. It did not specify which investors outside Switzerland could buy the fund.

"If investors want a US product, they have plenty of choice. If they want a non-US product in a neutral jurisdiction, until now they really didn't," said Cynthia Wu, co-founder and chief commercial officer of BIT. "BBIT gives investors outside the US a regulated, liquid way to hold Bitcoin through the bank or broker they already use, with the asset protection of a fund."

The Swiss Financial Market Supervisory Authority, or FINMA, approved BBIT on Oct. 20 after an 18-month review, according to BIT Asset Management. FINMA exempted the fund from diversification rules, allowing it to invest entirely in bitcoin.

Most bitcoin products listed in Europe are structured as debt securities, BIT Asset Management said, noting that BBIT is a Swiss investment fund. The firm said Swiss-regulated AMINA Bank holds the fund's bitcoin assets separately from BIT Asset Management's own assets. BBIT also allows in-kind subscriptions, letting investors exchange bitcoin directly for ETF shares without first converting it to cash.

"The economic exposure of a fund and a note can look very similar when everything goes well. The difference is what happens when it doesn't," said Friedrich Herzog, chief investment officer of BIT Asset Management. "The segregation of duties and responsibilities of counterparties is by design, and it is why products like this take years to build and approve."

BIT Asset Management was previously known as Crypto Finance (Asset Management) AG. BIT said the group acquired the Swiss asset manager in 2024 and renamed it Matrixport Asset Management AG before it took its current name.

The BBIT listing comes as bitcoin has fallen back below $60,000. U.S. spot bitcoin ETFs saw about $4.94 billion in net outflows in November through Tuesday, according to SoSoValue data. The U.S. ETFs began trading in January 2024.

Microsoft did not attribute the spy agency breach to any of them.

“ARTEX does not introduce new attack techniques; it uses common, pre-existing penetration testing tools and techniques,” Microsoft wrote.

The CIA intrusion, disclosed Tuesday, affected a shared intelligence analysis system that draws on sources such as social media, commercial satellite imagery, and data brokers. A source told Nextgov/FCW that the breach had been resolved and classified systems were unaffected. What information, if any, was stolen remains unclear, though such an intrusion could expose analysts' investigative priorities.

The NSA suffered a similar breach exposing unclassified information, according to the New York Times. Prior, the NSA's classified internal communications network was restored on November 20 after several days of disruption. Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton attributed the outage to software patching rather than a cyberattack. The Donald Trump administration has denied that the recent outages were part of a coordinated attack.

Separately, the FBI is investigating an apparent breach of its National Crime Information Center, a database used by law enforcement agencies nationwide that contains criminal histories, records of missing persons, fugitives, and stolen property. Investigators have not publicly established the extent of the intrusion or whether records were stolen.

Artex is not an AI model like ChatGPT's GPT or Anthropic's Claude. It is an agentic harness, a piece of software that lets language models interact with other programs and perform tasks rather than simply generate text.

A developer known as Autumn-27 published the project on GitHub in July. Written in Go, it was designed for penetration testing, the practice of attempting to break into computer systems with the owner's permission to identify security weaknesses.

The framework divides work among specialized AI agents responsible for planning, carrying out assessments, and reporting their results, according to Google's threat intelligence team. A shared record of findings helps the agents retain context and coordinate their work over lengthy assignments.

The underlying AI is interchangeable. Microsoft says Artex can use commercial and open-weight models, which means the framework is not necessarily subject to the safety policies of any one AI company.

Microsoft says that under certain conditions Artex can obtain lasting access with elevated permissions in minutes, rather than requiring someone to oversee each stage of an operation.

Artex attracted international attention in October after attacks on South Korean financial institutions. A November 13 FBI advisory linked the campaign to the theft of personal information belonging to approximately 67,000 people.

Autumn-27 removed the original repository in October following reports of criminal abuse. By early November, researchers had counted more than 1,600 publicly exposed Artex installations, according to the FBI, though that does not mean all were operated by criminals.

Removing an open-source repository does not erase the copies others have downloaded or the independent versions they have created. Microsoft says that this month Chinese cybersecurity company ThreatBook claimed ownership of Artex and began selling access to a commercial offering called Artex Pro.

The problem is not unique to Artex. Security researchers have long released tools that criminals later repurposed, but AI reduces the amount of manual work involved in running them.

The FBI has tracked Artex-related activity across 10 industries since August, including government, defense, finance, and technology.

On November 13, Amazon researchers described campaigns believed to involve Artex, including attempts to steal AI service credentials and circumvent identity checks at two cryptocurrency exchanges using deepfakes.

The identity verification system rejected every synthetic video attempt documented by the agents. Amazon also cautioned that it could not independently verify all the outcomes the agents claimed to have achieved.

As Decrypt reported last year, Anthropic said suspected Chinese state-sponsored hackers had already used Claude to automate 80% to 90% of the tactical work in a cyberespionage campaign targeting roughly 30 organizations.

Smaller criminal groups now have access to software that handles some of the coordination previously left to experienced hackers. They still need vulnerable targets, and defenders can still stop them.

Britain's National Cyber Security Centre said Tuesday that it had seen a sharp increase in AI-assisted attacks since September, with criminals exploiting familiar problems such as poorly secured accounts and misconfigured software.

For organizations defending themselves, the immediate priority remains fixing those weaknesses, reducing the number of publicly exposed systems, and improving detection. Britain's cybersecurity agency says today's agentic frameworks are relatively noisy, giving defenders a chance to spot them, though future versions may be harder to detect.

About 400,000 ZEC remains in the Sapling pool, worth about $291 million at current prices.

Zcash Zcash (ZEC) infrastructure team Zakura urged the network to accelerate the deprecation of its legacy Sapling shielded pool, citing speculation of mathematical breakthroughs at AI labs.

In a post early Thursday, Zakura recommended users migrate any ZEC still in Sapling to Ironwood. These shielded pools allow users to hold and transfer ZEC without publicly revealing transaction amounts or sender and recipient addresses.

"The time to prepare for a cryptographic breakthrough is before it happens," the team wrote.

While practical breaking of the pairing-based cryptography used by Sapling remains highly speculative, Zakura also recommended a network upgrade to disable payments into Sapling. Roughly 400,000 ZEC, or approximately 2% of supply, remains in the pool, according to Zakura, worth roughly $291 million at current prices. Zakura said most wallets support both Sapling and Ironwood, and the impact should be minimal, with miners accounting for much of the activity left in Sapling.

"Less than 2.6% of all transactions in the last 30 days use Sapling, and of those, 66% are known miner flows, and it's highly likely most of the remainder are miners as well," the team said.

An earlier Zcash forum proposal in April had suggested waiting a year after a community decision to make Sapling withdrawal-only. At the time, the proposal put its balance at 600,000 ZEC, down from 1.1 million at the start of 2024. Zakura did not suggest a new deadline in its Thursday post.

Zakura pointed to a reported proof of the Riemann hypothesis, which concerns the distribution of prime numbers, and unsubstantiated rumors that AI labs had also made advances in integer factorization, the process of splitting large numbers into their prime factors. The difficulty of that task underpins RSA encryption, which is rarely used in cryptocurrencies, according to the team. Zakura said some math can be used for attacks on both RSA and pairing-based cryptography, so advances in one could help with the other, but the reported Riemann proof and the rumors do not show that either can be broken in practice.

"Practical pairing breaks are highly speculative," Zakura said, adding that transparent transactions and Ironwood do not rely on factoring or pairings.

Nevertheless, a hypothetical break in Sapling's pairing-based proof system would allow forged proofs, Zakura said, putting the funds in the pool at risk. The same cryptography does not secure users' private keys or their cryptographic records of shielded funds, so the team said developers could replace the proof system without replacing those records. However, Zcash would have to freeze Sapling before an attack compromises its state and users could then later recover their funds using a new ECDLP-based or hash-based SNARK, Zakura said.

Separately, the Ethereum Foundation doubled its protocol security team, The Block previously reported, arguing that AI is a "more urgent risk" than quantum computing and recommending Keccak-256 over four competing candidates for Ethereum's planned shift to hash-based cryptography. Zakura said it is also working on a proposal to add hash-based, post-quantum signatures for Zcash transparent transactions using SPHINCS+ with 192-bit security.

#4782. Senate Democrats urge SEC to scrap crypto, tokenized stock exemptions

US Senators Elizabeth Warren and Chris Van Hollen, among others, have taken aim at two recent SEC efforts to ease regulatory requirements for the crypto industry.

US Senators Elizabeth Warren and Chris Van Hollen have urged the US Securities and Exchange Commission to drop a proposal that would allow eligible crypto projects to raise funds from US investors without registering their offerings and revoke an exemption for tokenized stock platforms.

In two letters sent to SEC Chair Paul Atkins on Tuesday, the Democratic lawmakers argued that the agency had exceeded its statutory authority in both cases and that the moves will put investors at risk.

“Together, the letters raise concerns about the SEC’s efforts to carve out special treatment for crypto assets and tokenized securities at the expense of investor protections and market integrity,” they said.

Both SEC measures drew crypto industry support, as they came at a time when the CLARITY Act struggled to advance in Congress. The Regulation Crypto Assets was first introduced in August when the landmark crypto legislation was stalled, while the tokenized stock exemption came out in September, two days after the CLARITY Act fell short of the 60 votes needed to advance.

The letters also come just a day after OKXICE, a joint venture between crypto exchange OKX and New York Stock Exchange parent Intercontinental Exchange, launched a round-the-clock trading venue for tokenized US securities under the exemption on Monday.

The tokenized stock exemption allows qualifying platforms to offer blockchain-based trading of tokenized US stocks without registering as exchanges.

SEC lists four other entities that intend to use the exemption, including TSV LLC (which commenced operation in early November), Kephas Corporation d/b/a Perpetuals.com, Formation Securities LLC and Fairmint TSV LLC.

Van Hollen, Warren and two other senators urged the SEC to withdraw the order, warning the order could create a “shadow stock market” that falls outside of regulatory protections.

“We are particularly troubled by the order’s sweeping exemption of TSVs from fundamental registration requirements,” they said.

They also argued the order places an “unreasonable burden” on publicly traded companies by allowing third parties to tokenize their securities unless the issuer objects within 30 days.

“This effectively establishes an opt-out regime in which companies must continuously monitor tokenization activity and respond to potentially numerous requests from different platforms to prevent unauthorized trading of tokenized versions of their shares.”

Related: Trump’s SEC nominee Johnson backs formal rulemaking for tokenized stock trading

The senators also argued venues are exempt from rules requiring them to display their best prices to traders. “These protections are foundational to the fairness and efficiency of our equity markets,” they said.

Atkins previously described the five-year exemption as an interim measure to allow onchain trading of certain US stocks while the agency considers longer-term rules.

In a separate letter, Warren, Van Hollen and Senator Tina Smith urged the SEC to withdraw its Regulation Crypto Assets Proposal, arguing that the proposal only serves to help crypto assets “escape” from the SEC’s regulatory regime.

The proposal would allow eligible crypto projects to raise up to $5 million over four years under a startup exemption or up to $75 million in a 12-month period under a separate fundraising exemption, without registering the offerings with the SEC.

The senators argued these exemptions would let crypto issuers raise money without prior SEC review, particularly the $5 million startup exemption, which would allow early-stage projects to raise money without providing financial statements.

“The proposal rationalizes the startup exemption with the idea that these offerings are from startups, and its only limitation is a $5 million offering cap. However, the exemption does nothing to actually protect investors – it simply means that the SEC is willing for investors to be defrauded in $5 million increments,” they said.

The SEC has previously said that the exemptions would require issuers to give investors written disclosures, and federal anti-fraud and anti-manipulation rules would still apply.

#4777. Another Bitcoin Mining Firm Flags 'Hashrate Hijacking' Attacks That Reroute Rewards

Another Bitcoin Mining Firm Flags 'Hashrate Hijacking' Attacks That Reroute Rewards

For the second time in weeks, a major Bitcoin mining firm has warned that attackers are siphoning mining rewards by hijacking the internet connections between miners and their pools, a sign that a long-dormant weakness in mining’s plumbing is now being exploited at scale.

Mining software firm Braiins said Wednesday that an attacker struck more than a thousand mining sites in a single second on Nov. 20, rerouting their connections to an impostor pool.

It follows a similar incident just last week, when mining-services firm Luxor reported that hackers had redirected miner rewards, which it tied to AI-assisted attacks.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short Bitcoin with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

The two firms described somewhat different mechanisms, but the effect was the same: hashrate quietly diverted away from the miners who produced it.

In its security alert, Braiins stressed the attacker didn’t need to break into any miner or into Braiins Pool itself. Instead, they exploited a long-standing flaw in Stratum V1, the unencrypted, plain-text protocol that carries work between miners and pools and offers no way to verify that the server on the other end is the real pool.

By rerouting traffic, the attacker impersonated the pool, fed miners legitimate-looking jobs, and pocketed the resulting shares under their own account at a separate pool.

The scheme hinged on manipulating the Border Gateway Protocol, or BGP, the trust-based system that tells networks where to route internet traffic. The attacker announced a narrower, more specific block of addresses that included a pool’s Stratum endpoint, causing networks that failed to validate the route to funnel miners’ connections to the impostor.

Hijacked machines kept hashing at full power while their pool dashboards showed zero hashrate, making the theft nearly invisible on-site.

Braiins traced episodes starting in early November across Latin America, mostly Brazil and Argentina, before a larger Nov. 20 wave hit mostly European miners, diverting between 0.6 and 1.9 exahashes per second at a time. The firm characterized the short, escalating bursts as the attacker “testing the waters,” noting the diverted hashrate grew more than tenfold in two weeks.

The technique isn’t new. Braiins noted that Dell SecureWorks documented the same routing trick stealing roughly $83,000 in mining rewards back in 2014, and the firm has warned about “hashrate hijacking” since 2020 as a reason to adopt the encrypted Stratum V2 protocol.

For years, the industry treated it as rare enough to tolerate; now, two firms in a matter of weeks have flagged it hitting miners in the wild.

Braiins urged the whole industry to act, recommending miners move to Stratum V2 or Stratum V1 over TLS with certificate verification, strip out plain-text backup connections, and push network operators to validate routes. It also released a free proxy tool for miners that can’t upgrade.

Any miner still on plain Stratum V1, the firm said, “is a target, on any pool.”

#4774. Tesla unveils 7.4 MW Powercore to take on ex-exec Baglino’s Heron Link

Tesla has unveiled Powercore, a solid-state medium-voltage transformer that also handles the inverter and breaker functions in a single unit. Tesla rates it at 7.4 MW (9 MVA) continuously at 34.5 kV, with grid-forming support up to 10 MVA of peak power.

It’s made in America and scheduled to start operating in 2027. That’s the same year Heron Power, the startup founded by Tesla’s former top engineer Drew Baglino, plans to start volume production of its own solid-state transformer, the Heron Link.

Update: Tesla has since released a full spec sheet for Powercore, including efficiency, warranty, and its data center plans. We’ve updated the article with the new details.

Tesla first said it would build its own transformers in September 2025, when it unveiled Megapack 3 and Megablock. Megablock connects four Megapack 3 units to a transformer and switchgear, but Tesla shared next to nothing about the transformer itself.

Powercore is that missing piece. Tesla announced it today through its Tesla Megapack account on X:

Introducing PowercoreSolid state medium voltage transformer, inverter and breaker – reliable, safe and secure7.4 MW/9 MVA continuously at 34.5 kVac w/ grid-forming support for 10MVA of peak powerMade in America. Operating 2027 pic.twitter.com/sHxqnpWJrf

About an hour later, Tesla followed up with a much longer post on X laying out the full spec sheet:

It also packs a built-in solid-state medium-voltage breaker that Tesla says clears faults up to 1,000x faster than a conventional breaker. There’s no flammable oil, and it’s modular, so components can be serviced in the field without swapping the whole unit.

Tesla is pitching one product for three markets: battery storage, utility-scale solar, and 800 Vdc data centers. For Megablock, Powercore replaces the current two-step setup, where Megapack’s inverters output 480 V AC before a separate transformer steps it up to medium voltage. Tesla says that old architecture had twice the losses. For solar, Powercore works as a central inverter for today’s 1,500 Vdc arrays and upcoming 2,000 Vdc systems.

Tesla still hasn’t shared pricing, customers, or a factory location. It only says Powercore will be made in the US “of U.S. and imported parts” with first units operating in 2027.

The idea behind a solid-state transformer is simple enough. A typical solar or battery project uses low-voltage inverters to convert DC into AC, then a big oil-filled, iron-core transformer to step that up to grid voltage. A solid-state unit does both jobs with silicon carbide power electronics, which means less gear, a smaller footprint, and active control over voltage and frequency. That control is what “grid-forming” means: the unit can help hold the grid steady instead of just following it.

And with lead times on conventional transformers stretching into years as data centers and renewable projects pile into interconnection queues, there’s real demand for an alternative.

You can’t look at Powercore without thinking of Heron Power.

Baglino spent 18 years at Tesla and finished as SVP of powertrain and energy, in charge of batteries, motors, power electronics, and energy products. He left in April 2024 and launched Heron Power in 2025 to build solid-state transformers.

He brought a lot of Tesla’s power electronics talent with him. As we reported when Tesla first announced its transformer plans, Heron hired engineers who led power electronics design for Powerwall 3, the next-gen Megapack, and Superchargers, along with the person who ran Tesla’s power electronics controls team for charging and energy products.

Since then, Heron has raised a $38 million Series A, a $140 million Series B led by Andreessen Horowitz and Breakthrough Energy Ventures, and a $60 million credit facility from J.P. Morgan and TriplePoint Capital. Former Tesla CFO Zach Kirkhorn sits on its board, and Tesla co-founder JB Straubel is an investor.

It’s also building Heron Factory One, a 286,000-square-foot plant in Morgan Hill, California, designed to make 10,000 Heron Links a year. That’s over 40 GW of annual capacity, with commercial production planned for late 2027.

And the customers are lining up. Vantage reserved more than 1 GW for its data centers, Intersect reserved 1.5 GW, LG Energy Solution Vertech is integrating Heron Link with its US-made battery systems, and RWE signed a pilot to install Heron Links at a Texas battery storage site in April 2027. Baglino says Heron has 50 GW of orders in the pipeline.

Here’s how the two compare based on what each company has disclosed:

On paper, Powercore is the bigger box, and now it has the better numbers too. At 7.4 MW continuous, it carries about 50% more power per unit than the 5 MW Heron Link, and its 98.86% peak efficiency edges out Heron’s 98.6%. But Tesla’s figure is a peak number, and Heron doesn’t label its own as one, so it’s not quite apples to apples. Neither company has shared pricing.

Tesla is also going straight at Heron’s data center pitch. Powercore converts medium voltage directly to 800 Vdc, the rack architecture Nvidia is pushing, and Tesla says it’s working with Nvidia on 800 Vdc designs. Heron’s data center version does the same 34.5 kV AC to 800 VDC conversion with built-in storage, and data centers make up about a third of its business. Tesla’s answer to the storage piece is Megapack on the DC bus, and it says it already has 10 GWh of Megapack running at data centers.

A big chunk of the people who designed Tesla’s power electronics over the last decade now work at Heron, and the guy who ran the whole org is its CEO. Tesla’s energy business also lost its longtime leader, Mike Snyder, last month, according to the WSJ.

This is all wrong. Tesla started developing this 3 years ago. Before Heron. The team selling Powercore is same as Megapack that has a way larger customer base than Heron. Also Heron is not a bankable company per project finance terms. So they will struggle to get projects financed through equity and senior debt . Not as Tesla

To be fair, Tesla still has plenty of power electronics expertise. Its silicon carbide inverters are in millions of cars and every Megapack. And it has something Heron doesn’t: a massive installed base and a sales channel. Tesla says it’s almost sold out of Megapacks for 2027, and bundling Powercore into Megablock is an easy upsell. Plenty of developers will take the one-stop shop.

Tesla’s specs now match or beat Heron’s on paper. But Heron has named customers, a pilot site with an install date, and a factory under construction. Tesla has none of those yet. I wouldn’t be surprised if Heron is actually ahead here.

But either way, the transformer shortage is big enough for both companies to sell everything they can build.

#4773. 1Password hacker stole customer names and emails, but vaults safe

The password manager, which is used by millions of people to store their login credentials, said customer vaults were unaffected by the breach.

Password manager 1Password disclosed Wednesday that an attacker stole names and email addresses belonging to some customers after breaking into its backend systems.

Customer vaults and their contents were not affected, but 1Password said the breach could lead to phishing attempts in the form of unexpected emails, texts or calls.

The company said it began investigating last Thursday after discovering signs an attacker had gained access to an employee’s GitHub account. The attacker used the account to access source code and push malicious code to backend services, allowing them to extract customer data.

“This data included customer names and email addresses, in addition to non-secret internal metadata about the account. At no time were customer vault contents accessed by, or available to, the attacker,” the company said.

The password manager lets people store passwords for different websites and apps in one encrypted vault. 1Password says millions of people and more than 200,000 businesses use its service.

The company also partnered with crypto wallet provider Phantom in 2022 to let users save their wallet passwords and recovery phrases in 1Password.

Following the attack, 1Password said it has since disabled the affected GitHub account, removed the attackers’ access, rotated all internal credentials potentially exposed, among other measures. It also said it has not found any evidence of user account takeovers or compromises from the attack.

#4771. Nearly 3 million pages of military records from the War of 1812 are finally online

🛍️ 200+ Black Friday deals actually worth buying 🛍️

Published Nov 19, 2026 2:01 PM EST

After 16 years of painstaking work, the National Archives and its collaborators have finally completed digitizing over 90,000 pension applications submitted to the United States government following the War of 1812. The project is more than just preservation for preservation’s sake. The roughly 2.8 million pages contain long-forgotten and missing details about 19th century Americans, their families, and their everyday lives.

While archivists previously digitized a similar collection related to the American Revolutionary War, the new documents will help fill in knowledge gaps between early 19th century military events and the 1850 federal census. Patricia Oxley, president of the Federation of Genealogical Societies (FGS), explained the project was also incredibly time-sensitive.

“In the specific case of the War of 1812 pension records, there is an added priority due to their frail state where not acting may mean sacrificing these for future generations,” Oxley said in a recent announcement.

The somewhat new United States of America declared war on the United Kingdom on June 18, 1812, citing objections to trade restrictions with France amid the Napoleonic Wars, as well as the Royal Navy’s impressment of American sailors. Although the conflict famously included a British attack on Washington D.C. that resulted in the burning of the White House and U.S. Capitol, little shifted geopolitically between the two nations following the ratification of the Treaty of Ghent on February 17, 1815. The U.S. tallied around 15,000 casualties, while the U.K. and Canada saw about 10,700 deaths. Another 9,000 Indigenous fighters died while enlisted between the two sides.

Today’s military records are meticulously documented and stored digitally, but applying for benefits such as pensions was a much more labor-intensive process during the 19th century. With the burden of proof on each applicant, veterans were required to supply lengthy accounts of their service. Each War of 1812 pension file is liable to contain not just combat information, but the names and personal details of fellow soldiers, family members, spouses, and countless other relations.

“Our users have been asking for the War of 1812 pension records for some time, and I expect this collection to be very popular based on the rich war time detail it contains,” added Brian Hansen, general manager at Fold3, Ancestry’s military records service and National Archives collaborator.

The collection also includes a full-text search feature using handwriting recognition technology. This lets users explore the files based on every named individual, and not simply the primary veteran applicants. The pension records are currently available for free on Fold3’s website, and are being added to the National Archives catalog on a rolling basis.

Correction 11/20/26 9:30 a.m. EST: A previous version of this article incorrectly stated the pension archive contained around 7 million files. This was based on an initial assessment from researchers in 2010. The article has been updated to reflect the more accurate tally.

#4768. BMW’s first US-built EV promises 456 miles of range and ultra-fast charging

The iX5 is BMW’s first fully electric vehicle built in the US, promising an estimated up to 456 miles of range, ultra-fast charging speeds, and plenty of Neue Klasse tech.

BMW officially opened its new Plant Woodruff in South Carolina on November 13, marking the start of series production of its sixth-generation (Gen6) electric vehicle batteries.

The Gen6 batteries will power BMW’s upcoming “X” electric vehicles, starting with the all-new iX5 SUV.

The iX5 is being built about 15 miles away at BMW Group Plant Spartanburg, the company’s first fully electric model to be assembled in the US.

BMW Plant Spartanburg is churning out around 70 iX5s a day following a $1.7 billion investment in South Carolina to expand the plant for EV production and build the new battery assembly plant in Woodruff.

According to Robert Engelhorn, president and CEO of BMW Manufacturing in Spartanburg, the company is confident the iX5 will attract buyers, promising 435 miles of range, ultra-fast charging, and its updated Neue Klasse technology and design.

Engelhorn told Automotive News in an interview that “there’s a clear trend globally for EVs,” adding that “We will contribute to this growth from the BMW side.”

BMW didn’t provide a specific production estimate for the iX5, but suppliers were reportedly told it would be around 60,000 EVs in 2027, down from 100,000 it initially forecasted.

“We said we would begin assembling fully electric BMW vehicles in the US by the end of 2026 – and we are delivering on that commitment,” Engelhorn said.

A company spokesperson confirmed that the iX5 will initially use battery cells from China before switching to US-sourced cells from LG Energy Solutions plant in Arizona by the end of the decade.

With production now underway, the iX5 is expected to begin arriving at US dealerships in early 2027.

The 2027 BMW iX5 60 xDrive starts at $79,800. BMW estimates the 144 kWh battery will provide up to 456 miles of range, up from the 435 miles it previously estimated.

It features BMW’s new “double-X” light signature, which combines the headlights, daytime running lights, side lights, and turn signals into one unit. The Double-X headlights come standard, but BMW said you can switch them for simpler diagonal stripes.

Last month, BMW showcased the i5’s ultra-fast-charging capabilities during a media event in Southern California with IONNA and Alpitronic.

During the demo, the iX5 60 xDrive hit a peak of 464 kW, which BMW said enables it to add an impressive up to 170 miles of range in 10 minutes.

The electric SUV features a dual-motor all-wheel-drive powertrain setup that delivers a combined 578 hp (425 kW) and 593 lb-ft of torque. BMW says it can go from 0 to 60 mph in 4.4 seconds and tow up to 6,000 lbs.

Inside, the iX5 adopts BMW’s Neue Klasse design and tech, like the smaller iX3 SUV. The setup includes a new 17.9″ infotainment touchscreen and BMW’s Panoramic Vision, which spans the bottom of the windshield. There’s also an optional 14.6″ passenger screen for a third display.

This is at the top of our short list. Out of Spec got 411 miles at 70 mph (by contrast the Gravity rated at 450 got 368 on the same run and the R1S rated at 410 got 349). It is a real 400+ mile vehicle with an ability to charge a real 300 miles in ~20 minutes.

Edit: OOS was with 22" wheels rated at 426. It should get >430 with the standard 21" wheels.

Measuring 197.2″ long, 78.7″ wide, and 68.9″ tall, BMW’s new iX5 is about the size of the Porsche Cayenne Electric.

By 2030, BMW plans to be assembling at least fully electric models at Plant Spartanburg. “This marks the beginning of the next chapter in the success story of the largest plant in our global production network,” Raymond Wittman, BMW’s head of production, said.

Following Debrecen (Hungary), Irlbach-Straßkirchen (Germany), and Shenyang (China), Woodruff is the fourth site in BMW’s production network to begin series production of the Gen6 batteries.

#4767. The 1Password Breach Didn’t Touch Your Vault. The Phishing Emails Might

The 1Password Breach Didn’t Touch Your Vault. The Phishing Emails Might

Password manager 1Password has disclosed a security breach in which an attacker accessed some of its backend systems and copied customer account information, though the company says the vaults where users store their passwords and other secrets were never touched.

In a disclosure published Tuesday, the Toronto-based firm said it began investigating on Nov. 19 after detecting that an attacker had gained access to an employee’s corporate GitHub account. The intruder used that access to reach

1Password’s source code and push malicious code to backend services, which then downloaded administrative data on a subset of customers. At no point, the company said, were vault contents accessible to the attacker.

Here’s what was taken, according to 1Password: customer names and email addresses, account and user identifiers, account creation and last sign-in times, public keys (which are public by design), certain protocol parameters that can’t be used to access an account, and non-secret internal metadata.

The attacker also copied source code from private repositories and gained access to the company’s software build systems, which hold some infrastructure credentials. 1Password said it has rotated all credentials that may have been exposed.

Crucially for users, the breach did not expose the data that actually matters: your vaults, the items inside them, the keys that protect them, or your account recovery keys.

1Password’s design means it never stores your account password or Secret Key, so an attacker who gets into its servers still can’t decrypt your vault. The company stressed there’s nothing you need to change in your account, and its apps and browser extensions are working normally.

What users should do, for now, comes down to what is generally good advice at all times: watch out for phishing emails, because they’re surely coming.

Because names and email addresses were exposed, affected users are prime targets for scam emails impersonating 1Password, particularly fake account-recovery or invitation requests.

The company urged caution with any unexpected message mentioning 1Password, and reiterated that it will never contact you to ask for your account password or Secret Key, which you should only ever enter in the official app or on the official site after opening it yourself.

One wrinkle involves emailed invitation and recovery links, which contain a token. 1Password said a small number of users in that state were notified directly; as a precaution, it lengthened the verification codes in those emails from six digits to ten alphanumeric characters to make guessing them impractical.

The incident echoes a run of breaches hitting companies that hold users’ most sensitive data, a pattern that has emerged this year as attackers increasingly target third-party systems and developer accounts rather than the encryption itself.

After the death of Shadow’s longtime partner Jackie in August, he had been spotted spending time with the 4-year-old banded female eagle named KD1 (later renamed Kaydee). Bald eagle mating involves a bit of aerial acrobatics—copulating pairs can be seen in what’s called a “cartwheel display,” in which they lock talons in mid-air while tumbling down to the ground. Male eagles do not have an external phallus, so mating occurs via a touch of cloacas. Vocalizations can typically be heard during the act, which lasts about 7 to 12 seconds, according to Raptor Resource.

As this is nature, we humans can’t predict or influence who Shadow will pick as a new partner. Or if he picks at all. All we can do is watch and wait and let nature take its course.
