#4700. Cournot Raises $5M to Build AI-Native Oracle for Verifiable Intelligence

Cournot Raises $5M to Build AI-Native Oracle for Verifiable Intelligence

Cournot, a startup building an AI-native oracle that helps applications and AI agents understand and verify real-world events, has raised $5 million in a strategic funding round co-led by Paper Ventures and Beam Foundation, the company tweeted on Thursday.

The firm was previously backed by YZi Labs, the investment firm of Binance founder Changpeng "CZ" Zhao, through its EASY Residency Season 3 program. Cournot said it will use the funding to develop its products, expand integrations on BNB Chain and other ecosystems, and move into areas including real-world assets, trading, parametric insurance, private credit and AI agents.

Cournot has raised $5M co-led by @papervc and @BeamFDN following earlier backing from @yzilabs through @EASYResidency S3, to build the verifiable intelligence layer for onchain applications and AI agents.

Cournot's mission is to expand what oracles can do: from structured data… pic.twitter.com/u0GnIBYFOO

— Cournot Protocol (@CournotProtocol) November 26, 2026

"As more financial activity and autonomous systems move onchain, the infrastructure around them needs to evolve beyond simply delivering data," Danish Chaudhry, founder of co-lead investor Paper Ventures, said in a statement. Cournot is making real-world intelligence "more verifiable, auditable, and usable by both applications and AI agents," he added.

Oracles bring outside information onto blockchains, so smart contracts can act on it. Most deliver structured data, such as asset prices. Cournot is aimed at questions that need interpretation, such as whether a real-world event has happened or whether the available evidence meets a contract's rules.

Its Resolution Oracle uses AI to judge whether defined conditions have been met, while its Intelligence Oracle provides probabilities, claims and supporting sources before an outcome is known.

Both products rely on a framework Cournot calls Proof of Reasoning, which is designed to show how an AI model reached a conclusion, rather than just the conclusion itself.

In a case study published in February, Cournot outlined a four-stage process. First, the system fixes what a question's terms mean before any evidence is gathered, and commits that definition as a cryptographic hash, so it cannot be reinterpreted later. It then collects evidence only from sources named in advance, within set time windows.

— Cournot Protocol (@CournotProtocol) February 7, 2026

Where a source may change, such as a government webpage, Cournot uses  zkTLS, a cryptographic technique that proves a website displayed certain information at a given time, to keep a tamper-proof record. Finally, the AI's reasoning can only draw on that verified evidence, and its verdict follows from the predefined rules, leaving a trail that can be audited and challenged.

The case study used a Polymarket market on whether there would be another U.S. government shutdown. Cournot has also cited a November 2025 shutdown market in which traders who correctly predicted the end date lost, because the Office of Personnel Management's website was updated a day after President Donald Trump signed the funding bill.

Cournot is also targeting the growing agent economy, in which autonomous AI agents need reliable outside information before making financial or operational decisions. Through its Intelligence Oracle skill, agents can request structured probabilities for events, the exact claims being assessed and supporting sources, and build those evidence-backed assessments into their own decision-making, according to the company.

As of November 25, 2026, Cournot’s Resolution Oracle had settled more than $1.41 billion in notional value across more than 29,200 resolutions, with 99.8% finalized without a dispute, the firm said. The company said resolutions had grown fivefold over the past three months and that the business is already profitable. Its oracles are used by prediction markets, agentic trading venues and trading card game platforms.

Its Intelligence Oracle Skill has scaled to more than 20,000 installs, 18,000 paying wallets and 967,000 paid calls, and the business is already profitable, according to Cournot. Its oracles are used by prediction markets, agentic trading venues and trading card game platforms.

Cournot argues the same problem applies well beyond betting, envisaging AI systems that could settle crop insurance by analyzing satellite imagery and local reports, or pay out on software contracts by reading a project's GitHub activity, with an auditable record of how each decision was reached.

"Human voting is slow and contestable, and black-box AI is fast but unaccountable," Cournot co-founder Daniel Wang said in a statement.

Cournot said that at no stage is an outcome decided by a token-weighted vote. That is how disputes are settled on prediction market Polymarket, which relies on UMA's Optimistic Oracle, a system that has drawn criticism after disputed outcomes. Polymarket has also integrated Chainlink data feeds for markets that hinge on asset prices.

Cournot pointed to a November 2025 post in which CZ said the industry needed more oracles, adding that "one or two is not enough."

In the longer term, the firm said its aim is to extend oracles beyond structured data into interpreting real-world events, providing verifiable intelligence and, eventually, taking action on behalf of AI agents within set policies. As more applications and autonomous agents operate onchain, the company expects demand to grow for infrastructure that helps them understand real-world information and weigh the evidence before they act.

#4695. BYD’s luxury SUV pulled a nearly 400,000-pound jumbo jet on just two wheels [Video]

Most SUVs are lucky to tow a small trailer without breaking a sweat. BYD’s new luxury SUV had a slightly bigger challenge: pulling a nearly 400,000-pound jumbo jet. And somehow, it did it on just two wheels. The video is worth a look.

The Bao 5 made its European debut at the Goodwood Festival of Speed (FOS) in July, the first SUV from BYD’s “premium technology-focused” brand, Denza.

As Denza’s first SUV designed specifically for Europe, Stella Li, BYD’s executive vice president, said the company is “confident that the Bao 5 will be a huge hit,” offering the perfect mix of off-road ability, luxury, and advanced technology.

The SUV uses BYD’s DMO (Dual Mode Off-road) plug-in hybrid powertrain, which BYD said is the “world’s first off-road-dedicated hybrid architecture/”

BYD’s off-road PHEV powertrain features three electric motors (one on each axle and a third generator) and a 1.5L turbocharged engine, delivering a combined 536 horsepower (544 PS) and 560 lb-ft (760 Nm) of torque.

BYD boasted that “Those figures – well clear of PHEV rivals’ and comfortably more than conventional diesel SUVs’ – are enough for a 0-100km/h time of just 4.8 seconds.”

To top it off, BYD added a double wishbone front and rear suspension with its DiSus-P intelligent body system, plus front and rear intelligent electronic differential locks with millisecond-level response to improve traction and performance.

The Bao 5 is equipped with a 31.8 kWh BYD Blade Battery that delivers a pure-electric WLTP range of up to 56 miles (90 km). And on a full tank and a full charge, the WLTP combined range is 537 miles (835 km).

To prove the new luxury SUV’s capabilities, BYD put it to the ultimate test — towing a Boeing 747 jumbo jet using just two wheels.

While pulling a 180-tonne, or nearly 400,000-pound, jumbo jet on four wheels is impressive in itself, Denza’s engineers wanted to push it further, doing something never tried before to showcase its off-road DMO technology.

The Bao 5 was put to the test at Dunsfold Aerodrome airfield in Surrey, England. It successfully pulled the jumbo jet in each of its three runs: one on four wheels, one on three, and the last on just two wheels.

Combined, the SUV towed the 747 for a total of 1,600 meters, or close to a mile, which BYD said is about four laps around a standard-size athletic track.

While a feat like this sounds impressive on paper, keep in mind that planes are designed to roll with as little resistance as possible. Top Gear pulled a 747 with a Touareg a while back. The main thing a pushback rig has is weight so that it can maintain traction. That's why BYD put nearly 10,000 lbs of ballast in the back - so it wouldn't spin its wheels on the tarmac.

It's still interesting, to be sure, especially removing two wheels.

BYD said the Bao 5 was a standard, production-spec Ultimate trim model, and the modifications were minimal.

A towing attachment was added, while the interior passenger seats were removed to make space for the 9,920 lb (4,500 kg) of ballast for the two-wheel pull test. In addition, Denza added small stabilizers to each axle so the vehicle remained balanced on two wheels.

After each run, the vehicle was inspected and confirmed to show no signs of stress on the powertrain, chassis, or tires.

The Bao 5 SUV normally has a towing capacity of over 5,500 lbs (2,500 kg), according to BYD’s Denza brand.

#4693. 7 bizarre things crypto whales spent a fortune on

The crypto rich have spent their fortunes on everything from dinosaur skeletons to rotting fruit, with some purchases defying belief.

They say a fool and his money are soon parted, but perhaps the idiom should be extended to crypto multi-millionaires and billionaires, who get their kicks from spending their fortunes on some truly bizarre things.

From a trip to space funded with Bitcoin to a $69 million nonfungible token, check out the seven weirdest ways crypto fortunes have been allocated so far.

For some early Bitcoin adopters, the ultimate luxury purchase wasn’t a Lambo or a Malibu mansion; it was a ticket off the planet.

In November 2013, British entrepreneur and Virgin Group founder Richard Branson announced that Virgin Galactic would accept BTC for spaceflight tickets.

At $250,000 a pop, the announcement piqued the interest of some of crypto’s earliest investors. In March 2014, Gemini co-founders Cameron and Tyler Winklevoss each purchased a ticket using Bitcoin to fund the space plunge — which they never actually took.

Bitcoin, space and beyond. Source: Winklevoss Capital

After stumping up 312.5 BTC each, the flights were repeatedly delayed until the Virgin Galactic VSS Unity was officially retired from spaceflight in June 2024.

Tron founder Justin Sun did make it into space briefly on Blue Origin in 2025 for $28 million, while f2pool co-founder Chun Wang actually commanded SpaceX’s Fram2 mission.

It was the first human spaceflight to fly over both poles of the earth. It’s not known how much he paid for the privilege but estimates suggest the four person mission would cost around $220 million.

Everyone’s heard of Bitcoin Pizza Day, when developer Laszlo Hanyecz infamously spent 10,000 BTC on two pizzas, but Bitcoin Banana Day gets considerably less attention.

Yet few examples capture the intersection of crypto and wealth quite like Justin Sun’s outrageous spend on, well, a banana.

Related: Pudgy Penguins expands retail footprint with Target trading card rollout

In November 2024, the founder of Tron paid $6.24 million for Italian artist Maurizio Cattelan’s Comedian, which consists of a banana duct-taped to a wall.

Sun subsequently followed through on a promise to eat the artwork, holding a press conference in Hong Kong where he took a bite out of the yellow fruit. If it were anyone else it might have been a Dada-esque artistic statement about the transience of worth in a consumption-based society, but it was Justin Sun, so it was probably just a publicity stunt.

He could have just gone to the 7-Eleven down the street and scored a banana for $1.50, but then he wouldn’t have been able to attract so much attention by eating it. The actual work he bought wasn’t the banana or duct tape, it was a certificate of authenticity for instructions on how to tape the banana to a wall.

Some people spend their fortunes trying to live more comfortably; others are more interested in the chance to live again.

Hal Finney, one of Bitcoin’s earliest contributors and the recipient of the first Bitcoin transaction from Satoshi Nakamoto, was cryopreserved after his death in August 2014.

Finney was a member of the Alcor Life Extension Foundation for more than two decades, and after his death, his body was preserved in the hopes that future medical technology might one day make revival possible.

Even better? Finney’s cryopreservation was paid for through a combination of life insurance and Bitcoin donated by fans. Crypto investor Peter Theil and “Bitcoin Jesus” Roger Ver are also set to undergo the process. Ver told Magazine back in 2021 he’d actually seriously considered killing himself and being cryptopreserved to be revived later, to avoid being sent to jail as a 23-year old.

Some collectors want paintings on their walls, others want bananas, and others still want something that has been dead for 69 million years.

In 2025, a group of investors, including Yoann Turpin, co-founder of cryptocurrency market maker Wintermute, spent $5 million on a dinosaur skeleton.

Yoann Turpin spent $5 million on a dinosaur skeleton. Source: Bloomberg

The Triceratops fossil is one of only two dozen or so known specimens, and was shipped from Wyoming to Turpin’s storage facility in Singapore.

Beyond the obvious novelty value, he reportedly said its appeal includes the fossil’s scarcity, which he likened to Bitcoin’s limited supply. One dino-skeleton will always equal one dino-skeleton.

From one enthusiastic collector of old relics to another. Patrick Gruhn, former head of FTX Europe, spent a chunk of his crypto fortune on a gold pocket watch recovered from the body of John Jacob Astor IV, the wealthiest passenger aboard the Titanic.

Related: 10 weirdest things ever tokenized... including farts

Gruhn spent $1.5 million at auction in 2024 and reportedly bought the old timepiece as a gift for his wife, partly because of his fascination with the Astor family’s history, and perhaps partly due to an affinity for sinking ships.

HEX founder Richard Heart’s taste in luxury goods could hardly be called understated.

In February 2022, he acquired The Enigma, a 555.55-carat black diamond, for approximately $4.3 million.

The enormous stone, also known as a carbonado diamond, is one of the largest faceted diamonds ever offered at auction, and the theories of its origins stretch from deep inside the Earth’s core to outer space.

Richard Heart bought a 555.55-carat black diamond. Source: Rapaport

Heart later renamed it the HEX.com diamond, connecting the unusual purchase to his cryptocurrency project. The US Securities and Exchange Commission launched a civil case in 2023 alleging that he misappropriated investor assets, including funds used to purchase the diamond. Heart was arrested in Turkey earlier this year due to an Interpol Red Notice connected to separate Finnish tax fraud charges.

What to buy for the person who has it all?

A $69 million NFT, perhaps. That’s what cryptocurrency investor MetaKovan paid in March 2021 for EVERYDAYS: THE FIRST 5000 DAYS, a digital collage by artist Beeple of 5,000 images created over 13 years.

At 42,329.453 Ether, the sale made it not only the most expensive NFT ever sold at the time, but also one of the most expensive artworks by a living artist.

The owner has no intention of selling the work, but it seems unlikely to fetch a similar price today. But he has purchased himself a notable place in art and crypto history.

Elon Musk Says ‘Multiplanetary’ SpaceX Could Be Worth $118 Quintillion. Yes, Quintillion

Forget becoming the world's first trillionaire, that’s spare change for Elon Musk.

The SpaceX CEO said Thursday that his company could eventually be worth a million times the current global economy, following an announcement that he and his company would give two SpaceX shares to every child in America.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short SPCX with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

“If SpaceX succeeds in making life multiplanetary and harnessing even a millionth of the Sun’s energy, it will be worth about a million times the current global economy,” Musk tweeted. “These are obviously absurdly difficult goals, but there is a path to achieving them.”

For those unfamiliar with numbers that large, the World Bank puts global GDP at $118.35 trillion in 2025. Using that figure as a reference, Musk is talking about a company worth roughly $118 quintillion.

“I recommend holding on to your shares,” Elon wrote.

If SpaceX succeeds in making life multiplanetary and harnessing even a millionth of the Sun’s energy, it will be worth about a million times the current global economy.

These are obviously absurdly difficult goals, but there is a path to achieving them.

— Elon Musk (@elonmusk) November 26, 2026

He didn’t disclose taking any substances before writing that tweet.

The figure Elon talks about is basically 118 followed by 18 zeros or approximately 68 million times SpaceX's current market capitalization. Comparing a company's valuation with annual economic output isn't an apples-to-apples comparison, but it illustrates the scale of Musk's ambitions.

The comments came hours after the Federal Communications Commission authorized SpaceX to deploy up to one million satellites designed to operate as solar-powered data centers in space.

It sounds cool and all, but capturing a millionth of the Sun's energy is a considerably more ambitious undertaking. The Sun generates approximately 380 septillion watts, meaning SpaceX would need to capture some 380 quintillion watts to meet Musk's goal.

As for the giveaway, SpaceX's official announcement specifies that its contribution will go to currently active Trump Accounts, tax-advantaged investment accounts for American children, with Musk personally matching the donation.

The combined pledge could be worth approximately $18 billion, per Reuters.

Musk has a peculiar relationship with big numbers and deadlines, especially when discussing the future of his own companies.

In 2016, the billionaire predicted that SpaceX could launch humans toward Mars in 2024, with the astronauts arriving in 2025. Humanity is not even close to that goal even this decade.

Three years later, during Tesla's Autonomy Day, Musk told investors that the electric vehicle manufacturer would have more than one million autonomous robotaxis on the road by 2020. Tesla was still preparing to launch its commercial robotaxi operations five years after that deadline.

During an earnings call in October 2022, Musk also said he saw a path for Tesla's valuation to exceed those of Apple and Saudi Aramco combined, which together were worth more than $4 trillion at the time.

More recently, he argued that artificial intelligence will surpass humanity's combined intelligence within five years, urging AI firms to cooperate on safety.

Musk's social media pronouncements have occasionally proved expensive, too. His infamous 2018 tweet about having secured funding to take Tesla private at $420 per share resulted in a $40 million settlement with the Securities and Exchange Commission, split evenly between Musk and Tesla. A jury subsequently found them not liable in a separate investor lawsuit.

Unlike his previous predictions, Musk hasn't given shareholders a deadline for reaching his astronomical SpaceX valuation.

He did provide a more terrestrial deadline for his stock giveaway, though. SpaceX's contribution is scheduled for December, with Musk's personal contribution following in June 2027, when the restrictions preventing him from transferring his shares expire.

Until then, two SpaceX shares are worth about $255.

#4690. Great horned owl survives 70 miles stuck in a moving truck

🛍️ 200+ Black Friday deals actually worth buying 🛍️

Published Nov 20, 2026 11:11 AM EST

In March, we reported on a bobcat who endured a four-hour surgery on two broken legs after getting hit and dragged by a car, after her head had gotten stuck in the car’s grill. During a strangely similar scenario, the same wildlife center in Pennsylvania recently treated a great horned owl (Bubo virginianus) who also got jammed in the front of a vehicle. But this one was dragged along for 70 miles.

“This is a very unusual case, as most animals that are hit by a tractor-trailer die due to their injuries or are killed instantly,” Tracie Young, director of Raven Ridge Wildlife Center tells Popular Science.

The wildlife center’s team received a voicemail from cargo and freight company Old Dominion Freight Line, saying that one of their drivers in Pennsylvania had hit an owl. When they called back, they discovered that the owl was alive and had gotten stuck in the truck’s air dam. The company’s maintenance team was able to remove the owl, but something was clearly wrong with the bird because it couldn’t fly away.

The wildlife team told them to place the injured animal in a dark and quiet place. Ultimately, transport volunteers were able to transfer the owl to Raven Ridge, where the team had waited to receive the patient past the wildlife center’s closing hours. Its feathers were a mess, but the staff was shocked to find no broken wings or legs, nor open wounds. The owl had just injured its left eye.

But when they called back the next day, “the story got even more incredible,” according to the wildlife center. The driver had felt the collision, but she didn’t know that the owl had gotten stuck on the truck, so she’d continued driving all the way back to the terminal.

“The distance from the spot where the owl was hit to the terminal was 70 miles,” the team wrote.“The owl was stuck headfirst in the fiberglass air dam for 70 miles at 65 miles per hour. It’s truly the luckiest owl we’ve ever seen.”

Staff brought the hardy survivor to their vet for an eye exam, which revealed blood and swelling in the injured eye. The wildlife team is now monitoring the bird’s recovery.

“The owl is doing great, and the left eye that sustained the damage is also healing. After we move the owl outside into a flight cage, we will make sure that the owl can sustain flight, that there are no obvious underlying issues, and that it can find the food placed in its cage,” Young concludes.

The goal is to ultimately release it close to where the collision occurred.

#4688. Volvo EWR150 Electric wheeled excavator gets to work in Luxembourg

As no-drip, low-noise job sites become more the global rule rather than the exception, Volvo’s incredibly versatile EWR150 Electric wheeled excavators are proving to be a smart addition to construction and municipal fleets – that’s proving true in Luxembourg, as well.

The Volvo EWR150 Electric wheeled excavator is helping the postage stamp nation of Luxembourg connect natural freshwater springs to a planned water reservoir, but the work has to be done in an existing groundwater protection zone, where even the smallest fuel spills or oil leaks could have serious consequences. An ideal opportunity, in other words, for a battery electric machine like the EWR150 Electric to shine.

“Sometimes I miss the sound of the engine,” says Thomas Weber, an operator on the project who’d previously worked with the conventional EWR150 wheeled excavator. “But the quieter operation of the EWR150 Electric is more beneficial for me, personally. Compared to the diesel equivalent, I find the performance and power to be identical.”

Volvo CE took to LinkedIn to share the work being done by the Luxemburgers at construction firm Elenz, touting the Volvo’s clean, quiet running in this highly environment.

For their part, Elenz executives are equally excited about the new machine. “Going electric is not a regulation, but a requirement for this particular job,” explains Christoph Schommer, Managing Director of Elenz. “We are thoroughly impressed by the EWR150 Electric. Its low noise level is a major advantage here. At the same time, the machine offers plenty of power and consistently delivers the same level of energy.”

The EWR150 Electric is built around a 270 kWh, 600V li-ion battery pack powering an electric drive motor that’s backed by a KERS-style hydraulic boom energy-recovery system that works like regenerative braking to extend the machine’s operating time. A 0.67 m³ (~0.9 yd³) bucket with 108.5-kN (~ 24,390 lb.) breakout force is standard, and offers a, 8.95 meter (~29 foot) maximum digging reach and 5.23 meter (~17 foot) digging depth. Volvo says the machine can typically operate for 8–10 hours depending on the application

Elenz is charging their EWR150 Electric overnight using a 32A L2 connection at a nearby sewage treatment plant, which also serves as the project office and a secure parking location for site equipment. By charging overnight, when Elenz’ crew isn’t working, the company has been able to integrate the big BEV without changing their existing work schedules.

#4686. Here’s what happened in crypto today

Need to know what happened in crypto today? Here is the latest news on daily trends and events impacting Bitcoin price, blockchain, DeFi, Web3 and crypto regulation.

Today in crypto, Vitalik Buterin called for verifiable chips to counter evolving hardware wallet threats, computer scientist Scott Aaronson warned that leading AI labs are likely sitting on undisclosed cryptography breakthroughs and US regulators authorized SpaceX to deploy up to 1 million satellites for orbital AI data centers.

Ethereum co-founder Vitalik Buterin on Thursday called for enhanced verifiability in computer chips, citing evolving security threats in the hardware wallet sector.

Buterin said in a blog post that most commercial open-source chips do not disclose enough detail to verify their physical construction. Publishing what a chip is programmed to do is different from providing a blueprint against which inspectors can check the hardware itself.

“This concern is not just theoretical,” Buterin said, adding that the crypto industry has seen attacks that involve inserting spy implants into hardware wallets before they get sold to consumers.

Buterin warned that future attacks could be harder to detect, with malicious functions built into replacement chips that resemble legitimate ones.

“This, you cannot detect with the naked eye,” he wrote.

Theoretical computer scientist Scott Aaronson says leading AI laboratories are likely sitting on undisclosed breakthroughs in cryptography.

In a blog post on Wednesday, Aaronson, a former OpenAI researcher and professor at The University of Texas at Austin, warned that algorithms emerging from AI-driven mathematical advances will eventually break currently deployed cryptosystems.

“I’m virtually certain, from multiple reliable sources, that the AI labs are now sitting on one or more bombshells in that area,” Aaronson said. “However, until I either see details or hear directly from someone at a lab, I feel much, much less confident about the specific nature of those bombshells.”

The remarks add to concerns that AI’s accelerating mathematical capabilities could eventually undermine the cryptography used to secure crypto wallets and blockchain transactions. Ethereum co-founder Vitalik Buterin and researcher Justin Drake raised those concerns in October.

The US Federal Communications Commission (FCC) has authorized Elon Musk’s SpaceX to deploy up to 1 million satellites as part of a planned network of orbital data centers, in what the agency described as a historic first.

According to a Wednesday FCC announcement, the satellite constellation, dubbed “Starmind,” is designed to provide orbital computing infrastructure to meet growing demand for artificial intelligence (AI), processing large amounts of data for use on Earth.

FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said the authorization opens a new frontier for computing infrastructure, as SpaceX and other companies seek to move data processing capacity beyond Earth. The agency said it is continuing to review additional orbital data center proposals.

The Starmind satellites will communicate with one another using optical links, with radio frequencies serving as a backup for communications and emergency operations. The FCC said the system complies with its orbital debris rules.

The FCC did not specify a deployment timeline or estimated cost for the Starmind constellation.

#4683. Tesla’s Semi Megacharger network hits 7 sites, far short of 37 goal

Tesla has opened its first Semi Megacharger in Texas, an 8-stall station in Mesquite on the east side of Dallas. With it, Tesla’s map now lists 7 public Megacharger sites and 44 stalls for its electric truck.

That’s progress. But with six weeks left in 2026, it’s less than a fifth of the 37 sites Tesla planned to have open this year.

Tesla Charging announced the new station on X on Tuesday night with its usual one-liner and a photo of the stalls at sunset:

New Tesla Megacharger: Mesquite, TX (8 stalls) https://t.co/UsCFMyCjo7 pic.twitter.com/W4G1e2BHkb

Tesla’s map lists the site at 2175 S Town East Blvd in Mesquite, with eight Megachargers rated at up to 1.2 MW each.

Texas is where Tesla has the most riding on this network. When Tesla added 64 Megacharger locations to its map in February, Texas got 19 of the 66 planned sites, more than any other state. Mesquite is the first of them to go live, and several other Dallas–Fort Worth sites are still marked “coming soon.”

The Pilot truck stop rollout hasn’t reached Texas either. When Pilot opened its first Megacharger in Georgia in October, it named a Flying J in Fort Stockton, Texas, as one of the next sites. It’s still not live on Tesla’s map.

Tesla also isn’t alone in DFW. Greenlane, the truck charging joint venture between Daimler Truck, NextEra and BlackRock, announced high-power sites in Dallas and Houston in May, open to any electric truck with CCS and MCS connectors. Tesla now has a station operating in the metro.

Here’s every public Megacharger currently live on Tesla’s map:

That’s 7 sites and 44 stalls in four states. When we counted in early October, there were four customer-facing sites with 26 stalls. Tulare opened the same week, Hodgkins came on November 10, and now Mesquite.

So Tesla is adding a site roughly every two weeks.

Tesla also runs private Megachargers for its own fleet at Giga Nevada and in Carson, California, and it sells Megachargers to fleets and depot operators through its business program. Forum Mobility switched on two at the Port of Long Beach earlier this month. None of those count toward the public network that Semi buyers without their own depot rely on.

Tesla’s Q4 2025 shareholder report showed about 37 Megacharger sites for 2026. Semi program lead Dan Priestley has said Tesla wants 46 by early 2027.

To me this seems like good progress, sure it's not right on time with their ambitious goal, but they are executing on their charging network and I'm sure more sites will keep opening.

To hit 37, Tesla would need to open 30 more sites in the next 43 days. At the current pace, it ends the year with around 10.

Pilot said in October that nine more of its sites were under construction, so a late burst is possible. But it would have to be a very big one.

And the trucks are starting to show up. Tesla launched volume production of the Semi in September at a Nevada factory it says can build 50,000 trucks a year, and it said last week that Chicago’s first 50 Semis are en route for delivery, a day after Hodgkins opened. Big fleets like that customer are installing their own depot chargers anyway, and most Semi charging will happen there. The public network is what lets a Semi leave its home region.

#4681. Nasdaq exec pushes for common EU rules on tokenized securities

Nasdaq’s Roland Chai backed exploring common EU rules for tokenized securities and said its Swedish subsidiary had applied for a DLT license.

Roland Chai, executive vice president and head of digital liquidity networks at Nasdaq, urged European Union lawmakers to explore creating a dedicated legal framework for tokenized securities to avoid legal uncertainties arising from fragmented regulations.

“We do see merit in exploring a 28th regime for dedicated, harmonized EU-level framework for tokenized securities issuance,” Chai said, speaking at the European Commission’s tokenization roundtable in Brussels on Thursday.

The term “28th regime” refers to the concept of an optional EU-wide set of rules that would apply alongside the national systems of the bloc’s 27 member states.

Chai said that Nasdaq’s Swedish subsidiary had applied for its first distributed ledger technology (DLT) trading and settlement license. Nasdaq was also considering accepting tokenized collateral, but faced constraints under current EU rules.

Chai’s comments echo a recent warning from European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde, who said Friday that Europe risks developing a fragmented tokenized securities market unless it establishes common standards. Without them, trading platforms could be unable to settle transactions with one another.

Related: Swiss central bank, UBS and SIX study ledger for tokenized settlement

BlackRock’s head of digital cash Hannah Winter said institutional clients seeking access to regulated money market funds were driving demand for tokenization.

“For us it’s absolutely demand-driven,” Winter said at the roundtable. “The ability to leverage a tokenized money market fund increases the return on those balances, but also frees up the ability for operations to be unlocked on a 24/7 basis.”

Winter said the primary uses of tokenized funds include treasury and liquidity management, as well as collateral for derivatives positions.

In August, BlackRock announced plans to offer tokenized versions of select European money market funds using JPMorgan’s blockchain infrastructure, including pound sterling, euro and US dollar share classes from BlackRock’s Institutional Cash Series.

BlackRock’s BUIDL fund, total assets under management and monthly returns. Source: RWA.xyz

BlackRock launched its first tokenized US dollar-denominated institutional liquidity fund, BUIDL, in March 2024. The fund had $1.55 billion in assets, down nearly 30% over the past 30 days, and a trailing one-year return of 3.59%, according to RWA.xyz.

#4680. Amflow launches its first city e-bikes, packing huge torque and serious smart tech

Amflow has made a name for itself in the electric mountain bike world with its high-performance Avinox-powered machines, but now the company is bringing that same technology to a decidedly more urban environment. The newly unveiled Amflow UE Carbon series marks the brand’s first move into the commuter e-bike market, combining a lightweight carbon fiber frame, powerful mid-drive motor, and a surprisingly long list of smart features designed for everyday riding.

And while these might look like fairly conventional step-through city bikes at first glance, there’s some seriously impressive technology hiding beneath those clean lines.

The new Amflow UE series comes in two versions, the UE Carbon and the higher-end UE Carbon Pro, both built around a full-carbon fiber frame weighing just 2.35 kg (5.2 lb).

The complete bike weighs as little as 20.9 kg (46 lb), which is fairly impressive considering the amount of hardware Amflow has packed into it, including front suspension, a suspension dropper seatpost, integrated lighting, and cargo racks.

Both models use the Avinox M2 mid-drive motor, which delivers up to 125 Nm of torque. That’s an enormous amount of torque for a city bike, and should make short work of steep hills, especially when carrying groceries or other cargo. And to put things into perspective, a lot of city e-bikes have barely 60 Nm for torque, so Amflow is knocking it out of the park for urban power.

A removable 600 Wh battery provides a claimed maximum range of 132 km (82 miles) in the lowest power assist mode, while fast charging can refill the battery in just 2 hours and 23 minutes.

The bikes also feature Avinox’s intelligent traction control system and a new Auto Boost function that automatically provides additional assistance when the system detects demanding conditions, such as accelerating from a stop or climbing a steep hill.

In other words, riders get much of the sophisticated motor technology developed for high-performance electric mountain bikes, but in a package designed for commuting to work or picking up groceries.

The bike is listed as weighing 20.9 kg (46 lb), though that figure conveniently excludes the front and rear racks, mudguards, pedals, kickstand, bike lock, bottle cage, and chainguard. So figure a few extra pounds for all of that gear, and you’re in the right ballpark.

The main difference between the two models is their drivetrain.

The higher-end UE Carbon Pro ($3,899) uses a customized three-speed electronically shifted internally geared hub paired with a Gates carbon belt drive. That should make it particularly appealing to commuters who want a quiet, clean, low-maintenance setup without worrying about chain lubrication or derailleur adjustments.

The more affordable UE Carbon ($3,499) instead uses a 10-speed electronic derailleur developed with TRP.

Both models support automatic shifting, allowing the bike to handle gear changes without requiring the rider to constantly think about them.

Amflow has also gone fairly wild with the technology integration.

There’s a 1.4-inch touchscreen display mounted on the handlebars, a wireless phone charging mount offering 15W wireless charging or 20W USB-C charging, and integrated lighting with automatic low-light activation and brake-sensing functionality.

The bikes even include a hardened steel frame lock on the rear wheel, Apple Find My integration, and a Lost Mode feature that can lock down certain components if the bike is stolen.

Apple Watch connectivity allows riders to check their bike’s status and unlock it, while heart-rate-based assistance can automatically adjust motor output to help riders maintain a target heart rate zone.

Some of these features, like the security and tracking, are immediately effective for nearly all riders, while other high-tech features like the heart rate-based pedal assist can provide even more functionality for niche riders looking to bridge the gap between riding for transportation and riding for fitness.

Of course, all the fancy technology in the world doesn’t mean much if a commuter bike can’t handle everyday errands.

Fortunately, Amflow appears to have taken the practical side seriously.

The bikes feature a low step-through frame, upright riding position, 65 mm suspension fork, and a suspension dropper seatpost offering 125 mm of height adjustment and approximately 30 mm of suspension travel.

The 26×2.0-inch Maxxis tires should also provide a comfortable ride over less-than-perfect city streets.

There’s a front rack rated for 20 kg (44 lb) and a rear rack rated for 27 kg (59.5 lb), with the latter supporting the MIK HD mounting system for compatible accessories, including child seats.

The standard frame is designed to accommodate riders from 155 to 190 cm (5’1” to 6’3”), while a smaller version for riders down to 140 cm (4’7”) is expected in 2027.

I’ve been impressed with the technology coming out of the Avinox ecosystem, and it’s exciting to see that technology finally make its way into a more practical city-focused electric bicycle.

As much as I love high-performance electric mountain bikes, the reality is that most people aren’t spending their mornings bombing down mountain trails. They’re commuting to work, dropping kids off at school, and running errands.

And that’s where electric bicycles can make an even bigger difference.

The Amflow UE series seems to take a refreshingly comprehensive approach to urban riding. The powerful motor is nice, but I’m arguably more interested in the belt drive, integrated security, cargo capacity, automatic shifting, and built-in phone charging.

Those are the kinds of features that can make an electric bicycle genuinely easier to live with every day. And as someone who actually commutes with an e-bike each day as my main form of transportation, these bikes are really speaking to me!

If you ask me, it’s great to see another high-performance e-bike manufacturer recognizing that the future of electric bicycles isn’t just about riding farther and faster on trails. It’s also about making everyday transportation better for the less exciting type of riding, too.

#4679. Tiny egg-eating snake discovered in Ethiopia

🛍️ 200+ Black Friday deals actually worth buying 🛍️

Published Nov 20, 2026 12:01 PM EST

Biologists have discovered multiple new species of egg-eating snakes slithering through the forests near southeastern Ethiopia’s Bale Mountains. Although researchers only described the white-throated egg-eater (Dasypeltis albigularis) in their study recently published in the journal Herpetozoa, they promised that information on additional finds is on the way.

“Three other species in this genus are still waiting in line,” Arthur Tiutenko, a study co-author and herpetologist at Germany’s Friedrich-Alexander University of Erlangen–Nuremberg (FAU), said in a statement.

Many snakes will snack on an egg if the opportunity presents itself. But for a handful of species, it’s all eggs, all the time. These nonvenomous snakes solely eat shelled embryos, and largely exist in Africa and some portions of India. To devour their meals, egg-eating snakes have evolved a set of very clever biological tricks. First, their back bones extend all the way into their esophagus and function like a saw to slice open shells. From there, the snake’s neck muscles contract and funnel the egg contents down its throat. Once finished, the reptile simply spits out the cracked shells.

However, Tiutenko’s team almost missed D. albigularis entirely. At first glance, the snake looks extremely similar to a species called the montane egg-eater (Dasypeltis atra). A closer inspection revealed some key differences—a patch of white scales extending down its stomach earned its “white-throated” moniker, while the skin between each scale has a distinctly blue shimmer. Other egg-eating snakes can rub their scales to create a rustling noise that startles foes, but only the D. albigularis females do the same—and they do it silently.

Don’t envision python-sized snakes chowing down on chicken eggs though. D. albigularis is less than eight inches long, weighs only 0.05 ounces, and is about as thick as a knitting needle. This means the snakes only have eyes for particularly tiny eggs from various diminutive birds. Luckily, their regional home is full of options.

“That may also be the reason why egg-eating snakes only live in Africa, and in particular in a small area in the southwest corner of the Arabian peninsula,” added Tiutenko.

#4678. A Complete Guide to Caring For Your Nails While Working Out

The gym: Great for muscle tone and cardiovascular health, less ideal for your nails. This advice will help keep your tips in top shape.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

THE ENDORPHINS, the physical changes you can see and feel in your body, the overall confidence boost that comes with doing something good for your body—yeah, the benefits of working out are hard to beat. The one area where a sweat session can fall short, however, is when it comes to the health of our nails.

If you're someone who loves a fresh manicure, especially one with some length, you know the struggle of keeping your tips intact at the gym. Between chipped polish, cracks and peeling, and the mental gymnastics of trying to avoid both, it can sometimes feel like your nails (and your sanity) are getting a workout of their own. “When I’m lifting plates or handling weights, I’m always conscious of how I’m gripping,” shares celebrity manicurist and KISS ambassador Gina Edwards, who's a frequent gym-goer herself. “I use my finger pads rather than the tips of my fingers to help avoid putting unnecessary pressure on my nails.”

Meet the experts: Gina Edwards is a celebrity manicurist and KISS ambassador. Dana Stern, MD, is a New York-based dermatologist who specializes in nail disorders. Marisa Garshick, MD, is a dermatologist based in New York City. Jin Soon Choi is a celebrity manicurist in New York City.

Not into manicures? Unfortunately, that doesn't mean you're completely off the hook. Even bare nails can take a beating: “The nail is a thousand times more absorptive of water than the skin,” says New York dermatologist Dana Stern, MD, who specializes in nail disorders. And because frequent handwashing and exposure to moisture often go hand in hand with working out, nails are subjected to expansion as they absorb water and contraction as they dry. “Repeated wet-dry cycles can contribute to splitting and peeling, particularly in people already prone to brittle nails,” Dr Stern adds.

But not to worry—you don’t have to choose between having polished digits and getting your fitness on. With a few smart habits, you can avoid all the pitfalls. Here’s how.

No matter how you choose to work out, there are plenty of ways your nails can suffer. And most of us don't even realize we're putting them in harm's way until it's too late. Maybe you're in a workout class, engaging in some friendly competition with your neighbor to see who can knock out their burpees the fastest, only to jam a nail as your hands hit the ground. Or perhaps the damage happens before you even break a sweat. Picture it: You're pulling on your most compressive pair of leggings when a nail snags on the fabric or, worse, bends backward and breaks.

Of course, some activities pose a more obvious risk than others. Exercises that involve “repetitive gripping, pressure, or friction, such as weightlifting, rock climbing, and certain types of strength training” can be especially hard on your nails, says Marisa Garshick, MD, a dermatologist based in New York City.

Here are a few of the ways your workout routine might be doing a number on them:

Handling dumbbells, weight plates, and other equipment can put pressure on nails, especially if they're long, dry, or already weak, says celebrity manicurist Jin Soon Choi.

Jamming a nail against a hard surface or repeatedly putting pressure on it can cause the nail plate to separate from the nail bed, a condition known as onycholysis. This can happen to natural nails, too, although extensions may create additional opportunities for snagging.

When a falsie gets caught on something, it can even cause the underlying natural nail to lift from the nail bed, explains Dr. Stern. Depending on the extent of the damage, it can take months for a healthy new nail to grow in.

Frequent handwashing and exposure to harsh cleansers (including those used to wipe down gym equipment and alcohol-based hand sanitizers) can contribute to splitting and peeling, Dr. Stern adds.

While running and cycling may be gentler on your hands, repeated pressure inside athletic shoes can cause bruising beneath the nail (known as a subungual hematoma), thickening, or even nail loss, explains Dr. Garshick.

The good news? Most workout-related nail damage is temporary, provided the nail matrix, which is responsible for nail growth, hasn't been damaged. But more serious injuries can have lasting consequences. A crush injury—heavy weight falling on a nail, for example—could cause permanent damage to the nail matrix, Dr. Stern says. Even when the damage isn't permanent, patience is key. According to Dr. Garshick, fingernails typically take three to six months to grow out, while toenails can take twelve to eighteen months.

The goal isn't to give up your favorite workouts or your favorite manicures. A few tweaks to your nail-care routine and how you handle equipment can make all the difference.

Here's what the pros recommend to keep your nails looking and feeling their best.

This ultra-nourishing product delivers a healthy dose of barrier-repairing ceramides, hyaluronic acid, and niacinamide sans greasy residue.

Jinsoon Primrose + Honeysuckle Healing Cuticle Oil

Choi recommends this product, from her own line, before bed to help maintain healthy nails and cuticles.

You’ve heard of bond builders for hair, right? This is the same thing, but for nails. It promises longer, stronger nails in just four weeks.

It’s important to keep in mind that Dr. Garshick says not every nail change is workout-related. Persistent discoloration, thickening, or lifting can sometimes indicate a fungal infection, psoriasis, or another nail condition. A new or changing dark streak, particularly one that doesn't grow out, should also be evaluated by a board-certified dermatologist.

At the end of the day, you don't have to choose between crushing your fitness goals and keeping your nails in good shape. In fact, Choi points out that exercise itself can actually be beneficial for nail health, as physical activity promotes healthy circulation, helping deliver oxygen and nutrients to the tissues responsible for nail growth.

It's the accidental injuries and repeated pressure that can cause problems, not the workouts themselves. With a few simple adjustments to your nail-care routine and a bit more awareness of how you're handling equipment, you can keep breaking a sweat without breaking a nail.

#4677. Ford’s first LFP batteries are en route, and the $30,000 Fathom EV pickup will get them first

Ford has entered the battery business. The first LFP battery cells are now rolling off the assembly line at Ford’s BlueOval Battery Park plant in Michigan and are headed to power Fathom prototypes in Kentucky.

How do you get more out of a battery without adding weight or more cells? According to Alan Clarke, Ford’s vice president of advanced development projects, who is also leading its Universal Electric Vehicle (UEV) platform, the answer lies in lithium iron phosphate (LFP) technology.

Unlike traditional lithium-ion, LFP batteries use no nickel or cobalt, which helps reduce costs. They also typically hold up better after years of use and charging.

To make it a reality, Ford turned to CATL, the leading global EV battery manufacturer. Ford uses CATL’s licensed technology and manufacturing expertise at its BlueOval Battery Park Michigan plant.

Ford said it will be the first in the US to deliver LFP batteries for mainstream automotive use, with the battery cells now rolling off the line in Michigan.

The first LFP battery cells are headed to Ford’s Louisville Assembly Plant and will be used to power Fathom prototypes, its first vehicle based on the UEV platform.

Ford designed and engineered the Fathom from the ground up for efficiency. As such, it chose prismatic battery cells because they fit directly into the chassis, reducing structural costs.

With cells now being delivered from a plant that it owns and operates, Ford said it will use the knowledge gained in Michigan to support more affordable EVs and Ford Energy, its new battery energy storage business in Kentucky.

At Ford’s new battery plant in Michigan, assembly lines can deliver 40 cells every minute, making it one of the fastest LFP prismatic battery assembly lines outside China.

Although the accelerated output drives down costs, Ford said employees use AI-powered image recognition and inspection tools to spot defects in real time and maintain quality.

“Our goal is to make defective cells so rare that we track their frequency per billion cells rather than per million,” Ford said.

With production testing now underway, Ford plans to have the battery pack plant in Michigan up and running in 2027, ahead of schedule.

Ford will open preorders for the Fathom in early 2027, starting at $28,350 for the standard-range model.

CEO Jim Farley said on the company’s third-quarter earnings call last month that the Fathom, Ford’s first vehicle based on the UEV platform, remains on track to launch in Q4 2027.

Farley said the Fathom is a “breakthrough product” that’s highly capable and still affordable. The starting MSRP is under $30,000, and the low cost of ownership is perfect for today’s market, he added.

Ford and Slate both producing vehicles with US-produced LFP batteries is a great milestone. Hopefully we can keep pushing our domestic battery supply chain forward.

Ford said the Fathom will offer more interior space than a Toyota RAV4, and it will cost less to own over five years than a three-year-old used Tesla Model Y.

The pickup will be the first vehicle to integrate Apple Maps directly into the navigation system. All versions will be BlueCruise-capable for hands-free driving, with standard Apple CarPlay and Android Auto, plus bidirectional charging capabilities.

Although we have yet to see it, Ford said the Fathom features a “large touchscreen display” with easy-to-use navigation.

Ford has not revealed battery specs or range, but we do know the pickup will have an NACS port after several prototypes were spotted at a Tesla Supercharger over the summer.

#4676. Spain Lets Its Financial Intelligence Unit Freeze Crypto Accounts Without a Court Order

Spain Lets Its Financial Intelligence Unit Freeze Crypto Accounts Without a Court Order

Spain's financial intelligence unit will be able to freeze crypto accounts it suspects are linked to money laundering or terrorist financing on its own authority, under a royal decree-law published in the country's official gazette on Wednesday.

The measure is tucked into a sweeping decree on consumer credit, which also caps interest rates on consumer loans and regulates buyers of bad loans. It adds a new article to Spain's 2010 anti-money laundering law, allowing the Executive Service of the Commission for the Prevention of Money Laundering and Monetary Offenses, known as Sepblac, to suspend or block a transaction in progress, or suspend the use of a bank, payment or crypto-asset account or a business relationship.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short BTC with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

Sepblac can act when it finds indications that the funds could be linked to money laundering or terrorist financing, in order to preserve them while it analyzes the case and, if its suspicions are confirmed, passes the information to the relevant authorities.

Suspensions of transactions can last no more than 10 working days, and suspensions of accounts or business relationships no more than five. When a suspicion stems from a suspicious activity report filed by a bank or other firm, Sepblac must order the suspension within three working days. Any suspension must be lifted earlier if it is no longer needed.

After those deadlines, a suspension ends unless a court ratifies or extends it at the request of the public prosecutor's office.

Until now, Sepblac could only suspend transactions at the request of financial intelligence units in other countries. Under the new rules, it can also act on its own analysis or at the request of Spanish police. Firms that fail to comply with a suspension order commit an offense under the money laundering law, while those that comply, and Sepblac itself, are protected from liability.

The government said the change brings Spain in line with standards set by the Financial Action Task Force (FATF), and transposes part of the EU's sixth anti-money laundering directive. The speed of financial transactions, particularly online, allows funds of possible criminal origin to be moved before authorities can finish their analysis, it said.

Sepblac handled 204 requests from other EU intelligence units to suspend transactions in 2025, more than double the 90 it received in 2023 and up from 175 in 2024, according to its latest annual report. The amounts involved fell to about €32 million ($35 million) from €92 million ($101 million), and the number of bank accounts affected slipped to 307 from 316.

Suspicious activity reports from crypto service providers rose to 1,672 in 2025, from 972 in 2024. Sepblac said those reports continued to reveal weaknesses in how crypto firms identify the parties to transactions, and named crypto, along with cash, as a key vulnerability, because of its pseudonymity and speed.

The new powers arrive as Spain prepares for its next FATF evaluation, with an on-site visit by assessors scheduled for February 2027 and a plenary discussion in October 2027, according to the watchdog's calendar. The FATF has flagged peer-to-peer stablecoin transfers as a top money laundering risk, and said centralized elements frequently persist in DeFi. In the UK, a taskforce convened by think tank RUSI has warned that crypto laundering is a material risk ahead of its own FATF review.

Other European countries are also expanding their powers over crypto. In Germany, lawmakers have backed giving customs officials powers to seize crypto and other assets of unclear origin.

The decree takes effect two months after publication. As a royal decree-law, it must also be ratified by Spain's Congress of Deputies within 30 days.

#4675. How To Build Strength You’ll Actually Use In Daily Life, According To A Trainer

Strength training isn't just about what you can lift in the gym. It helps make everyday tasks easier, whether that's carrying heavy shopping bags and moving furniture or putting a suitcase in the overhead compartment on a flight.

As we get older, we naturally start to lose muscle mass, strength and bone density—at approximately 3-8% per decade after the age of 30—but regular strength training can help slow this down, reminds Andy Carr, trainer and head of fitness for Snap Fitness UK.

Thankfully, you don't need complicated exercises to see the benefits.

By focusing on simple, functional movements that mimic everyday activities, you can build strength that carries over into daily life and keeps you strong, active and confident as you get older.

“It's not necessary to spend hours lifting weights to build strength that makes a difference,” he explains. “Even two or three strength sessions a week can help, especially when you're focusing on compound exercises that work several muscle groups at once.”

Squats are one of the best exercises for building lower-body strength because—as a compound exercise—they work your thighs, glutes, and core all at once.

“These are the muscles you use when getting up from a chair, lifting something off the floor or crouching down to do some gardening,” says Carr. Keeping them strong can make a real difference to how easily you move around, particularly as you get older.

Step-ups are great for building leg strength and improving balance at the same time, says Carr.

“They're particularly useful for everyday activities like climbing stairs, walking uphill, or stepping onto curbs. As we age, maintaining strength and stability in our legs becomes increasingly important, and step-ups are a simple way to work on both,” he adds.

Farmer's carries are a brilliant exercise for building strength you actually use, because they're essentially the same movement as carrying heavy shopping bags.

“They work your grip, shoulders and core, helping you carry things more comfortably and with better stability. Grip strength can decline with age, so it's a really useful exercise to include in your routine,” says Carr.

Picking something up, whether it's a laundry basket, a suitcase or a bag of compost in the garden, involves your glutes, hamstrings, and back. Deadlifts strengthen all these muscles, explains Carr.

“They're a great way to build strength for everyday lifting, so those jobs feel easier and you're more confident handling heavier objects.”

Rows are ideal for strengthening your upper back and arms, which we use for pulling movements throughout the day, from opening heavy doors to pulling a garden hose across the lawn.

“They also help support good posture, particularly if you spend a lot of time sitting at a desk,” says Carr. “Using a resistance band makes it easy to adjust the difficulty as you get stronger.”

Incline push-ups are a great way to build upper-body strength, working your chest, shoulders, arms, and core.

“These muscles help with everyday pushing movements, whether that's moving a shopping cart, pushing open a heavy door, or getting yourself up from the floor,” says Carr.

They're also easy to adapt to your fitness level, so you can gradually increase the challenge as your strength improves.

We use rotational movements more than we probably realize, whether that's turning to put something in the back of the car, reaching across to pick something up or digging in the garden.

Woodchops are great for strengthening your core and improving your ability to twist and turn with control, Carr explains.

“That becomes particularly useful as we get older, helping us stay mobile and making everyday movements feel easier.”

#4674. How EU brokers could lose access to Kyrgyz crypto exchanges

A vote on Kyrgyzstan could make an exchange’s home country the deciding factor in whether a European broker can use it to settle a trade.

A European Union sanctions list published in July has an empty annex for more countries, and Kyrgyzstan could be its first entry.

When authorities disrupted the Russian crypto exchange Garantex in March 2025, its employees set up Grinex, an exchange registered in Kyrgyzstan, and moved customer deposits there, according to the US Treasury. British sanctions officials later traced substantial transfers between Grinex and licensed international exchanges.

That episode may help explain why EU brokers may soon need to check where an exchange is based before placing a trade. In July, the EU gave itself the power to bar its operators from dealing, directly or indirectly, with crypto providers established in a country that systematically and persistently fails to prevent sanctions evasion through crypto services.

Related: Binance lists som-pegged stablecoin as Kyrgyzstan deepens crypto push

The EU left the country list, Annex LVII, empty. Kyrgyzstan is the proposed first entry, the Kyiv Independent reported.

As of Nov. 26, the proposal still needed unanimous approval from the EU’s 27 member states. If it passes, a European broker could check the name of a longtime settlement partner, find no sanctions listing for the firm, and still have to take its next trade elsewhere.

#4673. Black bear still catching fish despite broken arm

🛍️ 200+ Black Friday deals actually worth buying 🛍️

Published Nov 20, 2026 1:10 PM EST

Resilience and perseverance was on full display in Alaska this summer. The park rangers at Tongass National Forest in the southeastern corner of the state spotted an unnamed black bear (Ursus americanus) with a broken arm. Even with this injury, the tough bear still managed to catch the fish running through Anan Creek. For this grit, the rangers awarded the bear with the 2026 Grin & Bear It Award.

“We don’t know how the injury happened, but we’re impressed by the bear’s resilience,” the rangers write. “In other wild places the injury may have been a death sentence, but the abundance of Anan gives this bear a chance.”

Tongass National Forest’s rangers are awarding the annual Anan Bear Awards to the 39 bears spotted at the Anan Wildlife Observatory in Alaska over the summer.

The largest national forest in the United States, Tongass covers most of southeastern Alaska, including the state’s capital city of Juneau. The area also includes Mendenhall Glacier (a popular destination for Alaskan cruises), hiking trails, eagles soaring above, and plenty of bears. One of the hotspots is Anan Creek, home to one of the largest runs of pink salmon in Southeast Alaska. As such, the creek is a very popular dinner spot among black and brown bears.

According to Friends of Anan, 39 bears are known to feast on the salmon at Anan Creek. The population includes 31 black bears like the one with the broken arm and eight brown bears (Ursus arctos). Similar to their portly counterparts farther to the north in Katmai National Park, the bears return each summer to feast on salmon and teach their cubs how to fish in order to survive. And also like the fat bears of Katmai, every bear here has their own behaviors and quirks.

The U.S. Forest Service tracks and documents every bear spotted at Anan, while explore.org’s cameras broadcast live streams of their behavior.

#4672. West Coast Customs turns a Tesla Model 3 into a 1955 Chevy Bel Air

West Coast Customs has finished its first electric Chevy Bel Air, and there’s not much Chevy left under the paint. The Burbank shop cut the body off a Tesla Model 3, kept the entire rolling platform, and set a 1955 Bel Air shell on top of it.

The result, called Project B-Zero, looks like a ’55 Chevy from the curb and like a Model 3 as soon as you open the door. And it charges at Tesla Superchargers.

In the shop’s new video, “The First Ever Electric Bel Air,” founder and CEO Ryan Friedlinghaus explains that a longtime client, Troy Swope, wants to convert an entire car collection to electric and picked the Bel Air to go first. WCC had previously built the same client a Chevelle with a big gas engine.

Friedlinghaus, who drives a Tesla himself, decided against pulling the Model 3’s motors and battery out and fitting them into the old Chevy. Instead, the Tesla stays whole and the Chevy becomes the body kit.

That’s a formula WCC has used for years with gas cars. The shop calls it “old school meets new school”: an old GTO body on a new GTO, an old Camaro on a new Camaro, an old Mustang on a new Mustang. B-Zero is the first time it did it with a Tesla underneath.

“It sounds easy, but that process was tedious,” Friedlinghaus said.

Before any Chevy sheet metal went on, the crew took the bare Model 3 skateboard for a spin on the streets around the shop, with no doors, no lights and no seatbelts. Friedlinghaus joked about how many safety violations they were racking up. But it drove fine.

The real headache was the wheelbase. A 1955 Chevy rides on a 115-inch wheelbase, while the Model 3 sits at 113.2 inches. On its gas builds, WCC can cut, shorten or lengthen the newer car’s frame to match the old body. You can’t do that with a Tesla, since the floor is the battery pack.

So the shop changed the body instead, stretching the Bel Air’s rear wheel wells so the wheels sit where they look like they belong.

The client wanted the exterior to read as a mostly stock Bel Air. The original car was red, so WCC kept it red, with a satin finish and gloss black accents.

Inside, it’s a Model 3. The shop kept the Tesla’s interior, including the steering wheel and center touchscreen, and modified it to fit the Chevy body. The seats got black suede with white stitching in an octagon pattern that Friedlinghaus said was borrowed from the Lamborghini Urus, plus red accents and a “B-Zero” script on the dash.

Friedlinghaus said the goal was for people to see “a really nice Bel Air” from the outside, then open the door and find a Tesla. He also expects some double takes when it pulls into a Supercharger station.

He admits the reaction has been split. Plenty of people are mad that the shop electrified a Bel Air, and plenty of others think it came out great. The client is clearly in the second camp, describing the car as easy to drive and saying every trip in it feels like an event.

Here’s the full build video from West Coast Customs:

This is sick. I know Tesla doesn’t care about personal car ownership anymore, but they should really sell their platform so shops can do these conversions without using salvage vehicles.

Well I was really interested in this build until I read how they kept it entirely Tesla inside. Not at all what I was thinking or what I'd call a true old car conversion to EV. Instead, they simply transformed the outside of a Tesla into an old looking car. To me, even the outside looks too far removed from the original Bel Air and more like a street rod. If that's what the owner wants and paid for, great.

But for me, I would never do a conversion like that. I really want to convert an older 70's or 80's or early 90's Cadillac into an EV. But for me, I will insist that the outside and inside look 100% like the original car with just an EV powertrain.

Don’t get me wrong, if you can recycle a salvage, that’s good, but it can’t always be done.

Compare it to the 1966 Mustang that a Sacramento Tesla parts shop converted earlier this year. That project took about $40,000 and two years, with the team grafting sections of a Model 3 floor into the Mustang. It’s an amazing build, but it’s a lot of custom engineering. WCC’s approach skips most of that. You keep Tesla’s crash structure, battery thermal management, software, over-the-air updates and Supercharger access, because you never took the car apart in the first place. It’s closer to what S-Klub did with its Model 3-based Mercedes 300SL than a traditional drivetrain swap.

The purists will hate it. That’s fine. This Bel Air will get driven more in a year than most restored ones get driven in a decade.

#4670. Bitcoin Holds Above $60K as Death Cross Clouds Thanksgiving Recovery

Bitcoin Holds Above $60K as Death Cross Clouds Thanksgiving Recovery

Bitcoin and most major cryptocurrencies edged slightly higher Thursday as U.S. stock exchanges closed for Thanksgiving, a day after inflation data and fresh tariff concerns rattled markets.

Bitcoin traded at around $60,560 as of just after 1:00 p.m. ET, up 1.39% over the past 24 hours but down 3.67% over the past week, according to Decrypt's price tracker. The largest cryptocurrency has recovered roughly 5% from Wednesday’s low of $57,500.

Ethereum gained 0.87% to just under $1,700, while XRP and Solana rose 3.1% and 2.17%, respectively.

The Nasdaq Composite recovered from an intraday plunge of as much as 4.6% Wednesday to close down 0.62%. The S&P 500 contract for difference (CFD), a derivative tracking the index, was up 0.67% on Thursday at around 7,226 points, per TradingView. The cash index itself was not trading.

Wednesday’s selloff followed a combination of stronger-than-expected U.S. economic growth, proposed tariffs and renewed concerns over AI stocks, as Decrypt previously reported. Bitcoin’s daily chart looks considerably weaker than its stock market counterpart. Its 50-day exponential moving average (EMA) has crossed below its 200-day EMA, forming a bearish signal known as a death cross. Both averages are trending lower, with Bitcoin trading roughly 16% below its 50-day EMA of $71,478 and 19% below its 200-day EMA of $74,516, according to TradingView charts.

Neither crossover guarantees where prices will go next, but the comparison shows how much more technical damage Bitcoin has sustained. The announcement follows earlier reports of unusual charging and discharging behavior on the TM-B, which we previously highlighted as some of the growing pains facing Rivian’s ambitious new e-bike venture.

We’ve also reported on customers needing to return their bikes for repairs, raising questions about how smoothly the company’s initial rollout was progressing.

The issues align with many of our initial concerns we discussed a year ago when the bike was first unveiled, namely that the high-tech design means the bike incorporates many new and proprietary systems that could each lead to complicated and costly failures.

Now ALSO has officially acknowledged software problems affecting some bikes, including charging behavior, though it hasn’t detailed the full extent of the issues or confirmed whether they are directly related to those earlier reports.

I love the PR spin how only "some" bikes are affected. If it's the same bike running the same software, it's affected. The only bikes not affected are the ones that haven't been delivered, because they are not being used.

The bike represents a fairly radical departure from traditional electric bicycles, with proprietary technology throughout its drivetrain and control systems. That makes software an especially important part of the ownership experience.

To ALSO’s credit, pausing deliveries to fix known problems is probably the right move. Nobody wants to receive a premium-priced electric bicycle only to discover that it needs an immediate trip back to the manufacturer.

But for customers who have already waited longer than expected, another delay is undoubtedly frustrating.

ALSO says it will provide another update on November 24, hopefully with better news about when deliveries can resume.
